The geometry of the cone, Kimmell explained, allows oil to continue flowing around its edges while concentrating the sludge in the center, whereas a flat screen, with sludge spread across it, could completely clog the pipeline. Kimmell and Greenfield decided that the conical-filter idea was worth a try in blood vessels.

Sometimes concepts are the immediate, obvious implication of some newly discovered phenomenon or material. When William Perkin accidentally created a mysterious purple chemical when trying to synthesize quinine, he immediately saw that it might be useful as a dye. Similarly, when learning about electromagnetic waves, Guglielmo Marconi immediately saw that they might be used for communication. And the discovery of X-rays by Roentgen immediately prompted people to use them for medical imaging.

A concept will often be sufficiently obvious that it will be “in the air,” and the would-be inventor will inherit it rather than come up with it themselves. The concept of the incandescent lamp is sufficiently obvious once you know that running electric current through a resistor will make it glow that it was well established decades before Edison worked on the problem. Likewise, the basic concept of a heavier-than-air flying machine was in place for nearly a century before the Wrights mounted their attempt.

Different concepts might pin down the combinations and arrangements of the elements of an invention to different degrees. Some might be rather abstract, and some might be quite specific, though they almost never pin it down so completely that no subsequent empirical searching is required. The transistor, for instance, started with what was barely a concept at all — merely the idea that some sort of solid-state phenomenon could be used to construct an electronic amplifier — and it took years of studying solid materials and how they behaved before the specific phenomena that made it possible were uncovered. The concept of the pendulum clock, by contrast — using the (nearly) constant-time swing of a pendulum as the oscillator in a clock — pinned the specifics of the invention much more tightly. Often a concept lies somewhere in the middle, providing a general idea of how an invention should work but leaving significant blank spaces in how it will be implemented. Edison, for instance, started his hunt for a practical electric lamp with the high-level concept of using electric current to heat a filament to the point of incandescence, but there were many specifics that needed to be worked out. Edison’s first implementation used a platinum filament (chosen for its resistance to oxidation) connected to a temperature regulator, specifically because he wanted to avoid dealing with vacuums. Only later did Edison modify this arrangement to eliminate the temperature regulator and use a carbon filament in a high-vacuum bulb.

More generally, while having a starting technological concept doesn’t eliminate further technological search, it does considerably narrow it. Each phenomenon selected has specific triggering conditions: to get incandescence you need some way of heating your object; to get a population inversion you need the right sort of energy combined with the right sort of material. When Edison was creating his lamp he had a huge number of possibilities to sift through — different ways to prevent the filament from burning up, different materials that might be used as a filament, different bulb atmospheres — but it was massively reduced compared to a blind search through the entirety of technology space. Similarly, any existing technology that’s used as a component can be implemented in a variety of ways, but the range of possible variation is constrained by what’s needed to make that technology work. This kind of refinement is different than needing to make a discovery of a new phenomenon, wholesale. When Frank Whittle was working on his jet engine, he needed to build new, better compressors that were far more efficient than existing ones. But he wasn’t inventing a new type of compressor working on some novel principle: Whittle’s compressor worked more or less like existing compressors did and had a very similar arrangement of elements.

We can see the effects of this search space reduction using a PTOP (Phenomena Triggered by Objects with Properties) model — a model of technology inspired by Brian Arthur’s work, where different sorts of objects, with different sorts of properties, are placed in specific arrangements to trigger various phenomena, which then modify the objects in various ways. We’ll use the simple, linear PTOP model that we looked at previously. In this model, the goal is to create an object with the highest-level triggered property (P4), by placing the right objects with the right sizes in the right order. Even with this very simple implementation — 10 object types, 10 size values, and five objects that must be chosen correctly — there are 1 billion possible options. Guessing the entire technology at once randomly requires an expected 1 billion guesses, and even randomly guessing one step at a time still requires roughly 1,300 expected guesses.

But let’s say we have a technological concept guiding our search, telling us roughly how the technology we’re searching for will work. This hypothetical concept pins down the final phenomena exactly (we know the two object types and sizes that we need), but everything else is only narrowed a bit: we know the first and third objects’ types but not their sizes, and we know that objects 1 and 2 need to be equal in size. We can see that this basic concept provides a great deal of information, significantly reducing the expected number of trials required.

This level one search is so simple that it only barely resembles the search for a real technology (even very simple technologies in the modern age have more components and potential states), but we could conduct the same exercise with a larger and more complicated PTOP model and get the same results. A concept encodes knowledge about the world and how it works, and that knowledge narrows down the range of possibilities that must be considered when building a working technology. It may not fill in the blanks completely: the would-be inventor might have no initial idea how some step in his imagined process will work. Paul Lauterbur, for instance, had to make a “leap of faith” that there would be some way to recover the magnetic field strengths of individual coordinates to turn it into pictures. And Bell’s concept for the telephone was to use a varying electric current to carry voice along a wire, but he didn’t know how to produce that current and only stumbled across a method for doing so by accident. But a concept nevertheless makes the search process far easier, bringing it from “impossible” to “tractable.”

Technological concepts are, obviously, a product of our knowledge: knowledge of existing phenomena (such as the particle physics Townes used to create the concept for the maser), knowledge of existing technological elements (such as the knowledge of compressors and turbines Whittle used when creating the jet engine), and so on. This knowledge might be virtually certain, such as Edison’s knowledge of carbon’s melting point, or it might be only probable, such as the bet that there was a second histamine receptor that could be blocked by an appropriate molecule for ulcer treatment.

The knowledge that a would-be inventor has available to him acts as a sort of “palette” that he can draw from when coming up with ideas, and different inventors with different stocks of knowledge might proceed down different paths; historian Reese Jenkins notes that “[a]ny creative technologist possesses a mental set of stock solutions from which he draws in addressing problems,” (gorman and carlson 1990). Thomas Edison, for instance, repeatedly used mechanisms that he was familiar with in his inventions: Edison’s first kinetoscope used the same sort of rotating cylinder he had used in his phonograph. Likewise, in the race to build the first laser, every team attempting to build one was working off the same high-level concept but implemented it in different ways depending on their existing information endowment: the glass experts at American Optical pursued a glass laser, the gas experts at Bell Labs pursued a gas laser, ruby expert Theodore Maiman pursued a ruby laser, and so on. The more knowledge a would-be inventor has, the more possible options they have available to them, and the greater the chance they can come up with a workable concept: in the 1931 book “Industrial Creativity,” which surveyed 710 inventors on the characteristics that make for a successful inventor, “knowledge and memory” was the third most frequent characteristic noted.

When we looked at Brian Arthur’s technological evolution simulation, we noted that the key thing that made it possible to generate complex circuits randomly was modularity — combining simple elements into chunks, then making that chunk an element that could be directly manipulated and combined with other elements. Our knowledge of the world also has this basic structure: we can mentally manipulate things — concepts such as compressors, or motors, or resonant cavities — that are themselves arrangements of many individual elements, making it possible to orchestrate the arrangement of a large number of elements simultaneously.

Related to this ability to manipulate chunked information, some evidence suggests that strong mental visualization ability is an important characteristic for coming up with promising technological concepts. Inventors such as the Wright Brothers and Samuel Morse have been described as having exceptional mental visualization ability, and other notable inventors, such as Elmer Sperry, Oliver Evans, and Elihu Thomson, all described picturing a working invention in their minds before trying to build anything. Thomson stated that he “regard[ed] the imaginative faculty as chief in value to the inventor,” and that he never began a piece of work “in which I could not in my mind follow the whole thing through to an apparently satisfactory conclusion.” In “Industrial Creativity,” “imagination” was the second most frequently mentioned characteristic of successful inventors, losing out only to “perseverance.”

With mental visualization, together with the use of visual aids such as drawings, the inventor can to some extent “test” the workability of a concept, modifying it as necessary or discarding it for a new one without having to take the time and effort to build something in the real world. The Wright Brothers, for instance, initially considered a series of gears and shafts as a way to control their aircraft, but were able to foresee that its performance would be poor, and discarded it in favor of their famous wing-warping system without ever having built it. We can think of visualization as another way of processing a large number of elements at once. “A picture is worth a thousand words” is a saying for a reason: an image contains a huge number of relationships between different objects displayed that, thanks to our extensive neural machinery devoted to vision, we can process simultaneously and rapidly.

We can think of a technological concept as a region in technology space that’s promising to search. A good concept is one that both has a high probability of containing a working technology and has what we might think of as an easily traversable “technological landscape” — ideally, we’d like a region that, from a given starting point (a first attempt to build a working invention), we can improve the performance of the technology rapidly in as few iterations as possible, and that allows us to reach a very high level of performance without getting trapped in local optima.

There’s probably much to be explored about what sort of technological concepts will have these sorts of characteristics, but we can venture a few guesses. One key characteristic is that we’d like our technological landscape to give us information on how we should traverse it. Specifically, if you think of “technology space” as compressed down to a 2D plane, with the third dimension, height, representing a technology’s performance, we’d like to know the slope of the landscape, so we can walk uphill: make adjustments that will yield higher and higher performance. This, of course, is how machine learning works: gradient descent via backpropagation calculates the slope of the loss landscape and then walks downhill by changing the model parameters to move in the direction of lowest loss.

This sort of technological landscape doesn’t necessarily exist automatically. In “Inventive Minds,” a book about the nature of technological creativity, Harvard professor David Perkins talks about the concept of technological “Klondike spaces”: spaces that give little to no information on the direction to proceed:

Suppose you were searching for gold in the Alaskan Klondike at the end of the nineteenth century. The governing principle of your search would have to be, “Gold is where you find it.” You would look here, there, everywhere you could. You would be persistent, try different areas, and hope for the big strike. You would know a good deal about how to look, of course. You would know what kinds of rocks might bear ore. You would have a sharp eye out for the glint of gold in river gravel. You would search upstream from sites that showed some traces, in hopes of finding the mother lode. Despite this savvy, however, you would still find that most of your time was spent in searching rather than in systematically homing in on a find.Your search for gold is, of course, a special case of problem-solving. You are searching in the physical space of the Klondike, shifting from one position to another, exhausting dead ends, seeking new and promising terrain. Indeed, it’s useful to generalize the characteristics of this “Klondike Space,” because many other problem situations not so geological and geographical in nature have essentially the same logical topography. Many problem spaces, that is, involve punctuate targets with sharply defined boundaries (see Figure 13.1A), like a needle in a haystack or a few large nuggets or a hominid bone in a stratum. In such circumstances, it is difficult to move systematically toward a target. Rather, you find yourself casting about a lot. [My emphasis]

“Klondike spaces” are spaces where modifying a technology — making some part bigger or smaller, or faster or slower — doesn’t give obvious clues as to the direction of improvement. There are, broadly, two reasons this might occur. One is that a landscape might be highly uncorrelated — the performance of one technological option might have little relationship to adjacent options, so figuring out the local slope by making a small tweak and observing the change in performance doesn’t tell us much about which direction to head generally. When Edison was first hunting for a workable carbon filament, he found himself in this sort of landscape — he didn’t know which sort of carbon would work best, and just testing a material and seeing how long it lasted didn’t tell him much about the results he’d get from other materials, so he simply tested every type of carbon he had available to him until he found an option that was good enough.

The other reason that modifications might be uninformative is if the landscape is flat, and all nearby areas have the same performance. Consider, for instance, a string of Christmas lights where bulbs are connected in series, and every bulb needs to be working for the string to light up. If you plug the string in and it doesn’t turn on, you know that at least one bulb is burned out, but you don’t know which one, and testing one bulb doesn’t tell you anything about other bulbs or give hints as to which of them might be burned out.

An example of this sort of failure is Shockley’s first attempt to build a field-effect transistor in 1945; his theory of semiconductor behavior suggested a field-effect device should work, but extensive experiments with slightly different variations produced an effect “at least 1500 times smaller than predicted,” and he was forced to shelve the idea.

However, inventors are not simply at the mercy of these sorts of technological Klondike spaces; in practice it seems to be nearly always possible, with the proper knowledge, to determine a direction to proceed. This comes down to how we create concepts: a concept is based on some orchestration of phenomena whose behavior and triggering conditions are, to some extent, known; the individual workings of a technology can thus (in theory) be probed and experimented with to see whether the individual phenomena are behaving as expected, and give ideas as to the sort of modifications that are needed. Shockley’s failure to build a field-effect device suggested something was wrong with the existing theory of semiconductor behavior, which could then be tested and explored. Thanks in part to Shockley’s failure, it was eventually discovered that electrons trapped on the surface of a semiconductor (so-called “surface states”) were blocking the predicted field effect, a phenomenon that was then exploited to build the first point-contact transistor.

Similarly, Edison’s initial search for a carbon filament simply tested every carbon material that happened to be available, but careful examination of the materials tested suggested that materials that consisted of many parallel fibers performed the best — Edison later stated that paper was useless as a filament material because under a microscope it looked like “a bunch of sticks thrown together.” This initial search was followed then by a second, more thorough search that was focused specifically on fibrous carbon materials, leading to the bamboo filament.

This, I think, is one of the key things that technological concepts, and the knowledge that underlies them, do for the technological search process: they mean that the would-be inventor is never trapped in a Klondike space, and with the proper information and experiments can nearly always figure out a promising search direction.

We can similarly make some tentative conclusions about the sorts of technological concepts that might be improved upon rapidly, in as few iterations as possible. Something that has been demonstrated repeatedly is that the more modular the design of a technology is, the easier it is to improve rapidly. McNerney et al. 2011, for instance, used simulations to show that technologies with a greater degree of connectivity between components — the more the performance of one element was a function of other elements — had shallower learning curves and a slower rate of improvement compared to technologies with less connectivity.

But the most thorough demonstration of this effect I’m aware of is Stuart Kauffman’s NK model, developed to model fitness landscapes in evolution. In the NK model there are two parameters: N, which is the number of genes in some genome, and K, which is how much each gene’s fitness contribution depends on other genes. When K is 0, every gene contributes to fitness independently; if genes can have either a “good version” with a value of 1 and a “bad version” with a value of 0, overall fitness is just the sum of every gene’s value. But if K is 1, then the fitness of each gene depends on the value of one other gene; if K is 2 it depends on two other genes, and so on.

Increasing K increases the ruggedness of the fitness landscape. When K is 0, the landscape is smooth, there’s a single peak of maximum fitness, and it’s easy for evolution to walk up the hill to reach it. When K is very high, the landscape becomes, according to Kauffman, like “the surface of the moon,” there are a huge number of local optima, and finding the peak becomes very slow. From “At Home in the Universe”:

As the density of interconnections increases, changing a single gene (or bit in the program) will have effects that ripple throughout the system. It will be difficult indeed for it to smoothly evolve, with slight changes in the genome making correspondingly slight changes in fitness. So putting the effects together, as K increases, the heights of the peaks decrease, their numbers increase, and evolving over the landscape becomes more difficult.

We can demonstrate these same benefits of modularity with a PTOP model. The technology below is made up of 25 objects, arranged in five modules; each group of objects triggers its own series of phenomena, which modifies a different property in the final, output object. The goal of the technology is to maximize the product of all five output phenomena, which is achieved by dialing in the proper size for each object.

This implementation of the technology is highly modular; there’s little connectivity between the various objects/phenomena, and finding the maximum possible performance is relatively quick. This is the equivalent of a very low value of K in Kauffman’s NK model.

We can increase “K” by changing the nature of phenomena. In the model below, phenomena have a 40% chance to depend on the properties of multiple input objects, not just one, and these extra connections can be between any predecessor object, including ones in different modules. This makes it harder to find the best possible design, because hill-climbs now get stuck on local peaks. And the greater the degree of connectivity, the smaller the chance that the best design gets found. While in the unconnected version you could dial in each object’s size independently (smoothly climbing up the single peak), that doesn’t work when you start adding connections: you can’t simply dial in the optimum value at one spot and then move on to the next one.
So modularity doesn’t just make it easier to find working arrangements in technology space — it makes improving the performance of a technology far faster and easier.

Creating the concept is only the first milestone in the technological search process, and it’s my impression that it’s not a particularly binding step — if it was, I think we’d see a lot more inventions that could have been invented far earlier than we do. But it would nevertheless be useful if we could create technological concepts that reliably contained workable technologies capable of a high degree of performance. How might we go about this?

There have been various suggestions for these sorts of “invention algorithms.” One such algorithm has been suggested by Ed Boyden, neuroscientist and co-inventor of expansion microscopy and optogenetics. Boyden calls his method the “tiling tree”: break the problem down into the elements that it needs to contain and think of every possible way of doing each of them:

With optogenetics, my co-inventor Karl Deisseroth and I — when we were both students, we just started going through all the laws of physics. How would you control the brain? Well, there’s only so many kinds of energy. There’s mechanical force. There’s magnetism. There’s light. The list is pretty short, actually. You can actually try to write down every possible way of doing it. I call this method the tiling tree method, where you try to take this base of possibilities and break it down into parts.If you draw it properly, it looks like a tree diagram. Here’s this base of possibilities split into two parts, and each of those splits into more parts, and eventually it covers a page. It looks like a tree, and then the leaves of the tree — the bottom nodes — are ideas you could actually test by doing a literature search or doing an experiment. A lot of our projects, actually, at some point or another involve this kind of can-we-think-of-every-possible-idea approach.

Boyden points to Fritz Zwicky, a 20th-century astronomer, as the originator of this concept, who dubbed it “morphological analysis.” Here, for instance, is a chart showing a partial morphological analysis of different sorts of telescopes you might build:

In Zwicky’s version, the result is a “morphological box” — a multidimensional box where each axis is one category of variation the technology could have. So in the example above, you could have “unmanned, balloon-mounted neutrino detectors,” or “moon-based gamma ray telescopes that send telemetrics back to earth.” The goal of this sort of algorithm is to systematically list the different possibilities, letting you come up with concepts that you otherwise might have missed.

But the most developed method I’m aware of for coming up with technological concepts is called “TRIZ.” TRIZ, which is an acronym for “Theory of Inventive Problem Solving” in Russian, was created by Soviet engineer Genrich Altshuller in the second half of the 20th century. In the 1940s, Altshuller was in the Soviet Army working as an “invention inspector” and was tasked with helping inventors prepare patent applications and solve various problems related to invention. Having no good method for helping inventors with their problems, Altshuller eventually created one.

I would classify TRIZ as a sort of industrial improvement system, like Lean or Six Sigma or scientific management, with all that the designation implies. Having spent a lot of time studying industrial improvement systems, I think that they’re almost always based around some core insight or insights that are correct and useful. But they tend to put too little emphasis on building the intellectual foundations around these insights, and the insight tends to get applied in a “when you have a hammer everything looks like a nail” sort of fashion; practitioners are quick to take the insight out of its original domain and try to apply it as broadly as possible. Literature on industrial improvement systems tends to have “salesman energy,” implying the ability to solve all your problems with one weird trick. It’s often targeted at managers or other nontechnical people (and thus written in a less-than-rigorous way), and is often extolled by a sort of cadre of consultant-types that collects around the system, selling books and courses and offering cringey-sounding certifications. (So just as you can be a black belt in Six Sigma, you can earn the title of TRIZ Master.) In my experience there’s often value in extracting the actual valuable information embedded within industrial improvement systems from the consultant slop that accretes around them — my book “The Origins of Efficiency” is in some ways one big exercise in doing this — and I suspect TRIZ is similar.

TRIZ is, essentially, based around the idea of technological search. Altshuller breaks new inventions down into five categories, based on how difficult the search process is for coming up with the idea for them. Level 1 inventions require simply small variations of an existing idea and can be discovered easily after a few trials. Level 2 inventions are slightly more complex and might require 10 to 100 different ideas before an engineer discovers a workable concept. At level 5, the most complex, the unaided inventor might require 10 to 100,000 trials, or perhaps might never discover a workable concept, because it requires a fundamentally new phenomenon that the inventor isn’t aware of. The greater the level of invention, the greater the knowledge needed to find a good concept.

The basic thesis of TRIZ is that by default people do not search for concepts very efficiently; they try different arrangements of elements based on their own experience or simply try and combine ideas by pure trial and error in the hopes they might work. This sort of search process might work for the simplest level 1 and level 2 inventions, but it’s inappropriate for the more transformative inventions of the higher levels. TRIZ is in large part devoted to getting people to think in new ways to come up with more promising concepts, sort of in the tradition of brainstorming or Oblique Strategies. Altshuller notes Zwicky’s morphological analysis as a way to generate new concepts that’s better than people’s default methods, but thinks it’s insufficient in part for combinatorial explosion reasons: the more axes of possibility you add, the more possible options you must consider, and the number of variants quickly gets enormous. An invention with merely mid-level difficulties, Altshuller notes, might have millions of possible variations to consider.

Instead of enumerating all possible concepts, TRIZ focuses on using tools to come up with better concepts. The heart of this is what’s known as a “technical contradiction.” Per Altshuller, the fundamental difficulty in coming up with a good technological concept is conflicting requirements: increasing performance along one axis might require raising some value, while increasing it along another axis might require lowering it. For an airplane, getting it into the air is aided by decreasing the weight, but making it strong enough to withstand the forces subjected to it is aided by increasing the weight. In Altshuller’s view, the creation of a new invention fundamentally requires some way of overcoming this contradiction, so you don’t have to sacrifice one measure of performance for another.

To overcome these technical contradictions, TRIZ provides several tools, chief of which is its list of 40 principles: a list of heuristics for how to rearrange the elements of a concept to eliminate the technical contradiction. Principles are things like “segmentation — divide an object into independent parts,” “prior counteraction — preload countertension to an object to compensate for excessive and undesirable stress,” and “asymmetry — replace symmetrical forms with asymmetrical forms.” These principles are, supposedly, based on analysis of tens of thousands of patents to determine what technical contradictions are encountered in practice and what methods can be used to overcome them. There’s an involved algorithm for applying these principles called ARIZ, but in essence a would-be inventor first imagines the most perfect, ideal version of an invention, a North Star to navigate by. He then determines the technical contradiction at work preventing him from achieving the ideal version of the invention and consults a “contradiction matrix,” which states which principles might be applied to resolve it. Properly applied, this results in the generation of a better concept that pushes an invention toward its ideal state.

I don’t necessarily think TRIZ holds the key to understanding the nature of invention; like with any industrial improvement system, I think it’s probably a mix of valuable ideas, exaggerated benefits, and consultant drivel. But I suspect there’s some promising work that could be done by analyzing the various elements of TRIZ — the ARIZ algorithm, the contradiction matrix, the list of principles, and so on — to try and understand more about the nature of technology space and how it might be searched effectively.

For instance, many TRIZ principles suggest pushing some particular parameter higher or lower: making air more reactive (principle 38) or less reactive (principle 39), changing the degree of feedback (principle 23), amplifying a harmful factor (principle 22), and so on. (In fact, principle 35 is just a bunch of parameters you might try changing.) This reminded me of a bit from Richard Hamming’s “The Art of Doing Science and Engineering,” where he notes that in high-dimensional spaces, almost all the mass of an object is concentrated near the surface, which suggests that for any given design of an object the optimal design will have some particular parameter pushed as far as it can go.

Similarly, one of the steps in one version of the ARIZ algorithm is applying the “size time cost” heuristic — imagining the invention with size, time, and cost pushed either toward zero (as small as possible, a process as fast as possible, or a cost as cheap as possible) or toward infinity, and imagining what the solution looks like under these modified constraints. This is a specific example of a more general idea, expressed in Judea Pearl’s book on problem-solving heuristics, that search heuristics are often developed by thinking of ways to solve simplified versions of the problem (such as problems with various constraints eliminated or added).

The first milestone in creating some new technology is the creation of the technological concept: some basic idea of what arrangements of phenomena and objects will, together, create a working technology. This doesn’t eliminate the search problem — many of the most famous inventors, such as the Wright Brothers and Thomas Edison, faced most of their difficulties once the concept was in place. But the concept transforms what would be an impossibly difficult search problem into one that’s far more tractable.

articles.title: AI researchers debate what we should do next – Daniel Kokotajlo and Ege Erdil
articles.titleZh: AI researchers debate what we should do next – Daniel Kokotajlo and Ege Erdil
articles.summary: AI researchers debate what we should do next – Daniel Kokotajlo and Ege Erdil

blocks.text: New podcast episode between Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo. I thought this was going to be a debate, but they ended up agreeing on a lot more than I expected.

Their main point of disagreement is how likely it is that we get some intelligence explosion that gives us AIs more competent than any human expert before 2029. Ege puts this possibility at around 20%, whereas Daniel thinks it’s higher than 50%.

They agree that there is not a huge difference in probability, and that, in either case, the situation is crazy enough that our civilization really needs to grapple with how the world might be transformed, and we need a plan that actually makes sense.
In particular, we should stop antagonizing China if we think some kind of global treaty will be needed to make superintelligence go well.

There was another important crux about how well we should expect future AIs (that swamp humans in population size and cognitive power) to treat us, and how relevant it is that current AIs, by and large, seem to be pretty nice.

We close off with predictions for 2027. Daniel, of course, expects superintelligence next year. Ege’s median for full automation is 2040, but by next year he expects AIs that can beat any video game on Steam, and which can control robots to get simple physical tasks (like folding laundry) done at roughly human speed.
Watch on YouTube; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify.

0:00:00 – Will we have superintelligence by 2029?
0:04:31 – Why Ege thinks it’s too early to pause
0:13:46 – The adversarial stance on China is dangerous
0:19:30 – There is no plan, because people are in denial
0:29:37 – Misalignment itself will slow down RSI
0:40:52 – Will superintelligence be like descendants or invaders?
0:48:47 – Will AIs care about humans by default?
0:52:39 – Will AIs become less nice as they get more powerful?
1:01:08 – People are in denial about how good AI already is
1:09:01 – Predictions for 2027
1:23:38 – Is AI research actually verifiable?
Dwarkesh Patel
Today, I’m joined by Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo. Ege is a researcher at Google DeepMind. Daniel is one of the authors at the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027 and AI 2040.

I wouldn’t call this exactly a debate, because I hope it’ll be more of a discussion. But there is a set of key disagreements you guys have, which leads one of you, Daniel, to believe that AI is likely to kill us all within the next few years, and Ege, you to believe that will not happen. I feel like a big crux in this conversation is just timelines. How soon do you expect extreme superintelligence?
I’ve articulated, and Paul has articulated in the last episode, why there could be extreme superintelligence soon. Ege, why do you think that’s unlikely?
Ege Erdil
The main difference between me and Daniel, and also between me and Paul, is just how much you believe in the software-only singularity.

This is the idea that you have a fixed pool of compute and a roughly fixed amount of data that is at least not synthetic. Then what happens is that you get better AIs. Those AIs are able to use that pool of resources way more efficiently to make progress on AI research, and you get this feedback loop that at least goes for many orders of magnitude before it fizzles out. Then that improvement is so big that you get, I don’t know, 10 years of progress in six months or whatever, something like this.

I think the evidence we have is not sufficient to give high credence to that. Maybe that’s 10-20% likely to happen over the next three years. That’s probably the biggest disagreement, where Daniel thinks that’s over 50% likely.
Dwarkesh Patel
Why do you think it’s more than 50% likely that there will be extreme superintelligence within the next few years, whereas Ege thinks that’s 10-20% likely?
Daniel Kokotajlo

First of all, I don’t think that we will probably all be dead in a couple years. The thing I would say is, unless we substantially slow down the AI companies, then probably we will lose control and there will be misaligned AIs running the show in a couple years. It seems like we’re getting close to fully automating the AI research process. That would be the main claim. How close? It seems like it’s going to happen in 2027. Maybe not, maybe 2028, maybe 2029, but I would say it’s slightly more likely than not in 2027.

Once you have fully automated the AI research process, things will probably accelerate. More likely than not, they will accelerate a lot, as Ege was describing, although I do think there’s some uncertainty there.

Then I think that a lot of the limitations of current AI systems, such as the data inefficiency or whatever, will melt away relatively quickly as progress accelerates dramatically. You’ll end up with AIs that are able to flexibly learn quickly from all sorts of experience. You might call them top-expert-dominating AIs, perhaps. Top-expert-dominating AIs are effectively superintelligence as far as I’m concerned.
Dwarkesh Patel

Here’s a naive question. We go back five years and we have AI systems that can’t even hold a conversation. Now we have systems that are solving Millennium Prize Problems. They’re pretty good coders, et cetera.

If we just go another five years of progress at this pace, do you think it’s likely that that alone gives us AIs that are competitive with human experts? If we’re looking forward five years, do we even need that much RSI?
Ege Erdil

We might not, but I think it’s unclear. If we don’t get any RSI, my median timeline to everything being automated and humans having nothing to do — they’ve been completely automated — is something like 15-20 years from now. That’s a median timeline. So in the next five years, you still have to give it 20% or something that it could happen. I think that’s a very live possibility.

While there are disagreements about software-only singularity and similar things, in some sense those disagreements don’t matter that much. All I’m saying is, Daniel is saying something is 50-60% likely to happen over the next three years, and I’m saying it’s 20% likely. That question might be interesting. But even if it’s only 20% likely, if the situation is very bad, you should still do something about it.
So even though it’s maybe a larger disagreement numerically, I don’t think it’s a significant disagreement qualitatively.
Daniel Kokotajlo

So the reason why you’re working at Google instead of protesting outside of Anthropic, which is a practical difference between our behavior, is less to do with the probabilities on the different scenarios and more to do with… Well, what actually? I’m curious.
Ege Erdil

Several things. In this particular question of whether a pause is a good idea or not, I’m worried about any plan that involves us acting on risks before we have seen some significant version of the costs in the real world. Right now, the thing people always cite in these discussions, since some number of months ago, is the Hugging Face incident. But I personally think the Hugging Face incident didn’t cost that much and was a pretty small incident in the grand scheme of things. It was much less significant than a plane crash in terms of the cost imposed.

I do see it as analogous to if you have a new technology, like nuclear reactors or aircraft or whatever, and you haven’t actually seen anything significant go wrong, but you have all these theoretical arguments for why things might go wrong, and you’re intervening on the basis of that… I’m just suspicious about that approach in general.

The thing I’m challenging when I say that is the view that the way you get aligned AIs is to have some theoretical breakthrough in alignment. Nothing in machine learning has worked like that. Machine learning is not a field that has large theoretical breakthroughs.

There have been no large theoretical breakthroughs over the past 10 years. All of them have been incremental. You stack this compute multiplier on top of this compute multiplier, and you get this efficiency gain. It’s just very incremental. There are a lot of dimensions that you optimize at once. That’s the way you make them more capable.
So I don’t see why you would assume anything different about the way we would make them more aligned.
Dwarkesh Patel

This is maybe a key disagreement between you guys. Are there tractable interventions that we could make? Specifically, are those interventions more tractable if we get more time to make them, interventions that are likely to increase the value of what these AI systems do and how they treat us?
The AI Futures Project has just put out a pacing scheme that you say will delay the intelligence explosion by a year, which you are expecting in 2027. So you think this would slow it down to 2028?
Daniel Kokotajlo
Something like that. We have uncertainty, but yeah.
Dwarkesh Patel
What changes if we get the intelligence explosion in 2028 rather than 2027?
Daniel Kokotajlo

A couple things. First of all, I think that progress is being made on AI alignment and the science of understanding how AI works and all sorts of things like this. It’s not going fast enough, but it is being made. Each additional year of time that we buy, there’s additional progress, which cuts away at that probability mass of the bad outcomes happening.

The second thing I would say is just general awareness, what you might call AGI-pilling of society and of government. This might actually be the most important thing. Most people just don’t really take this stuff seriously, don’t really understand what’s happening or what’s coming. That seems broadly bad to me. We’d probably be in a better situation if more people in general understood what was coming.
I think that process is happening. It might even be happening exponentially. Every year that goes by, more people learn more, more people pay attention, more people start getting involved.
Ege Erdil

It’s just very difficult without tangible things that the technology does in the world to wake people up to its potential. For example, if we pause at the current level of capabilities, let’s assume we do that. Yes, this process of people waking up continues slowly. But just look at the skepticism in the financial markets about the viability of this technology. There’s huge skepticism. That’s also probably just shared broadly throughout the public.

The public doesn’t really like AI. They don’t really like data centers and stuff. But that’s not because they realize what’s going to happen. They just have a much more myopic distaste for it. If we pause now, then people are still not going to understand what’s at stake. The public conversation about this will still be very poor because it will be operating from bad premises.

There’s an advantage to getting the capabilities to a point where it’s evident to everyone that if we keep going from there on, the world will be totally transformed. Because doing this through ordinary persuasion is extremely difficult.

You might get some kind of pause politically, but it would be supported by factions who don’t actually agree with your worldview. They would support it for some other reason. They don’t like big tech companies. They don’t like the fact that all these companies are constructing all these data centers that the local communities they’re in don’t support. It would be for some other reason and not for the reason that you think is most important.
Daniel Kokotajlo

I technically agree with you, but in spirit disagree. Maybe one way of modeling it is something like: for each new AI capability that appears, there are some rapid updates that people make immediately just upon learning that that capability exists. But then there’s a whole bunch of additional updates that get made as that capability gets more deployed into the world and so forth.

Right now capability progress is moving fast enough that we still haven’t nearly exhausted the gains in awareness that would come from just deploying the current capabilities more. If we had a pause where we continue to deploy the current capabilities but not make them smarter, we would continue to see significant gains in awareness over the course of several years. Then it would taper off after more than that.

I do think that things are going fast enough now that to a first approximation, the wake-up is a function of serial time rather than a function of the capabilities. Although there’s some function of the capabilities.

Another thing I would say too is that a lot of the people who have anti-AI opinions don’t share my worldview and don’t have anti-AI opinions for the same reasons as me. But that’s also changing to a larger extent. We’ve seen multiple senators and congresspeople come out and say, “AI could kill us all,” and, “The AIs could go rogue,” and things like that. That’s mostly happened just in the last year.

So that too is trending in what I would consider the right direction, where people are waking up and understanding the magnitude of the situation more. I don’t think it’s trending fast enough in the right direction. I don’t think that it’s going to be where it needs to be in 12 months, but in 24 months maybe, or in 36 months maybe.
Ege Erdil

I agree with the point that if you pause now, you will still get an increase in awareness for a couple more years. But given the distance between where we are now and where I think people need to get, given the implications of technology, I think that’s just not going to happen if you pause at the current level of capabilities.

It might be enough. You might have the view that the current level of support and current political coalitions or whatever are sufficient to get a pause to happen. Then that has the benefits that you care about, that it slows things down, even though it’s not done with a complete understanding of what’s going to happen and it’s done for different motivations. It’s a defensible position.

I’m just worried in the longer term that if we as a civilization just insist on being irrational about this topic, then we will just make a lot of bad choices, a lot of choices that don’t make that much sense. It’s important that people understand that in some ways, the world we’ve been in is going to no longer exist in some sense.

Even if the outcome is very good for us, if you get Daniel’s ideal outcome or something like that, that world is still completely different from today’s world. People don’t realize. Maybe if they realize, they’ll be like, “Wait, we don’t want that world. That doesn’t fit our preference. We want some other world.”

But if there is never an explicit conversation that has the correct factual premises about what’s going to happen, then we will just not be in control of the situation. Because even though in some sense we are in control, in the sense that all the relevant decisions, at least for a while, are being made by humans, they are not being made as a result of some rational deliberation.

I’m really worried about that. Some random thing is going to happen, and we won’t control what happens. It will not be the output of any process that makes any sense. Then we will have to live with it. That’s very scary.
Daniel Kokotajlo
That’s a reason to go slower in AI development.
Ege Erdil
It’s a reason to go slower after sufficiently many people are aware of the potential of technology.
Daniel Kokotajlo
And you think it’s too early for that?
Ege Erdil
I think it’s too early.
Daniel Kokotajlo

Then what about, instead of going to a complete pause, going slower? Say we do the thing where we restrict AI R&D compute to 10% or 5% of the company’s compute. This slashes the overall pace of progress by a factor of two or three or something.
Perhaps you would agree then that because you are still making forward progress, you are still going to get the levels of awareness eventually.
Ege Erdil

A couple things about that. First of all, I don’t know how to get international coordination for this. Given what we’re currently doing, it’s going to be very hard because the US is being quite adversarial against China right now, especially with recent events. That just seriously undermines the possibility of getting any coordination. It’s actually very myopic and dangerous. They really have to stop doing that.
Daniel Kokotajlo

One of the nice things about the 10% idea is that it would still leave the US companies with about as much compute on AI R&D as the Chinese companies. Also, because a lot of Chinese progress is just coming from the US, you wouldn’t even need a deal to do this level of pacing.
Ege Erdil

For now, but that’s because China is behind on a bunch of the industrial tech that’s required to produce a lot of compute. For example, they don’t have access to EUV machines and stuff like this. The US has been able to get the Netherlands to successfully export control those and so on. But given China’s rate of economic growth and industrial progress, these are temporary advantages. So it gives us some time.

China is not going to be able to catch up in five years, probably. So if you think five years is enough, then you can get five years with a method like this. But if you think we need 15 years or something like that, then I become more pessimistic.
Dwarkesh Patel

Or let alone some global agreement. In the limit, it is worth discussing. If you really believe we’ll have such powerful AI systems, this depends on what you think the nature of destructive technologies is. But it is plausible that you might need some global treaty on, “Hey, you can’t have superintelligent systems that you’ve deployed to go research mirror life or something.” At some point, there’s not just a race. Unless you think you’re just going to literally outcompete every single country.
Daniel Kokotajlo
I agree that ultimately, if we want to have a good future, we’re probably going to need to make some sort of treaty or deal with China and other countries, something like that.
Ege Erdil

If you’re really worried about that risk, there has to be coordination with them. There’s no way to avoid that. You can try to delay things. You can have a five-year lead. You have five additional years. That buys you something. But if you’re really worried about that risk, they could try to build it in five years. It’s not that long.
Any prospects of coordination with them, I think, are being severely damaged by the policy of the US government towards China, and also, to some extent, of Anthropic towards China.
Daniel Kokotajlo
I agree with that.
Ege Erdil

This is very short-sighted. It’s because people don’t understand the stakes of the technology. The awareness that this is a world-transforming technology that completely changes the condition of civilization is just not there.

We have to figure out a way to deal with it, and there’s no way to adequately deal with it without some kind of coordination. And people are torpedoing the prospects for doing that for some very short-sighted, short-term gain of, “Oh, we get a couple years’ additional lead.” It doesn’t make sense, what people are doing. So I think they’re operating from a very different view of what the technology will be like, which I think is going to have bad consequences.

This is another thing I think is not being discussed, even in communities where people are trying to think of, “How do we win? How do we get the safe AI first?” Gwern had an interesting comment about this, I think on LessWrong, where he asked the question: let’s say the US wins. We get our superintelligence. Then what?

What do we do? Do we do some crazy operation to try to overthrow the Chinese government or something like that? If they think that’s what the US is going to do, what are they going to think of any attempt to try to coordinate with them to get a slowdown? They’re inherently going to be extremely suspicious of any such attempt if they think that is the plan.
Dwarkesh Patel

I think people correctly point out that I have too many people on my podcast who have this particular view of AI trajectories, and not only AI trajectories, but the implications of that trajectory. However, it does end up being the case that when you talk to a skeptic, for example, Ege, it seems like you just have slightly different probabilities on things. The people who totally dismiss this altogether, I feel like, don’t have reasonable arguments about why AI capabilities will not continue.

If you take seriously the possibility of minds in data centers that learn like humans and which will swamp us in population, thinking speed, agglomerated experience and expertise, et cetera, no people who take that seriously, at least so far as I’ve found, put less than 10% or less than 5% that things go pretty badly for biological humans.
Ege Erdil

This is something I try to emphasize. By people who don’t have enough context on the situation, or who are not carefully reading what I’m saying, I could be considered this person who disagrees with Daniel, that I give 2-3x less probability to various things compared to Daniel or something like that. That’s actually not that important in some sense.

There are some things for which a 3-4x difference can make a difference. If you think the risk of doom right now is 4% a year compared to 1% a year, that can actually make a difference for whether you think we should pause or not. That’s because you’re comparing it to the 1% per year of people who are dying. Then whether you think the risk per year from AI is higher or lower than that is an important analytical question.

But compared to the people who just don’t take the technology seriously, or who have what I would call magical views about the human mind, which are very widespread, all of those people are just in a different world. They’re not actually engaged with what’s happening.

If they were making predictions over the past few years, or past five years or whatever, they would’ve been very, very, very wrong. All their predictions would’ve been completely wrong. Often they don’t make predictions, so they’re not proven wrong.
Dwarkesh Patel
Actually, should we discuss what you, Daniel, predicted in AI 2027, which was released in the beginning of 2025? What did you predict that the world would look like in late 2026?
Daniel Kokotajlo

The biggest thing that was incorrect was that we said China wakes up in summer of 2026. There has been a lot of wake-up, so to speak, in China. They’ve started talking a lot more about existential risk and alignment and superintelligence and things like that, but not to the same extent that we predicted.

As far as we know, they haven’t gotten the state seriously involved in their AI projects and started funding them more, sharing algorithms and things like that, and merging compute. That’s definitely one thing we got wrong.

Some of the stuff we got right was relatively obvious, like the rise of agents, the rise of coding agents in particular. For early 2026, the title of our chapter there was “Coding Automation,” which coincided very nicely with Claude Code taking off.
Ege Erdil

The revenue projections, if anything, were slightly pessimistic, in the sense that they were lower than what ended up happening. But at the same time, by end of year, the market projections seem like they were too optimistic.
Daniel Kokotajlo
We said 30% or something.
Ege Erdil
Yeah, and if anything, it might end up being down, or only slightly up. A bunch of AI stocks are down, Nvidia’s down, and so on. That’s an interesting thing to also maybe talk about a little bit.
To me it looks like there is a big cleavage in worldviews that’s happening here between people in finance, people in New York, and people in San Francisco, maybe is one way to put it.

People who are viewing these as just ordinary stocks see a lot of business risk. They see a lot of default risk on debts. The business plan doesn’t seem very sustainable. The companies are burning a lot of money. Even Anthropic still has negative margin, or maybe very, very slightly positive margin. So it seems very risky, and they’re like, “Can this really go on for another one or two years?” But here people say, “In one or two years, we might all be dead.” That’s a very big difference in views.

Most people in the world, most people who have a lot of money or whatever, still don’t believe any of this, basically. Not only do they not believe what Daniel is saying, there is just a general complete skepticism of the technology, despite what has already happened.

People still don’t, as far as I can see, just buy this premise. Humans are physical objects. We have some capacities. The brain has some capacities. It’s just a physical object. We have enough resources to reproduce what it does. Then that’s obviously going to have completely transformative implications.
That argument is very straightforward. It doesn’t really hinge on these details about exactly when it happens, but people just don’t believe it.

It seems to me like this very deep-rooted irrationality that is tied to maybe lingering notions of the human soul or whatever. There’s a lot of this going on where people don’t want to confront the reality of what’s happening.

The basic thing is that there is a massive transformation that’s going to happen. And you need to understand it’s going to happen if you want to talk about, “What do we do? What do we change? How do we adapt to it? What is our plan?” We have no plan right now. There’s nothing.

The fact that people will be superseded as the things that produce economic value, that has dramatic implications. People don’t think that’s going to happen, so they’re doing nothing about that either. There’s just a bunch of ways in which, with this transformation of the world, we should be talking about what we’re going to do. And we’re not doing that because people don’t think it’s going to happen.
Dwarkesh Patel
Not only that, but when you do talk about it, there’s just a huge backlash. I think it’s just very psychologically disturbing to take this possibility seriously.

I released this article about the Hugging Face incident where I summarized the story. There was a huge backlash to the fact that I used the word “civilization” in it to describe these agent swarms. At the time I thought to myself, “I would have never guessed that this would have happened. But if I had anticipated it, maybe I could have just avoided using that word, so people could actually read what happened and understand the incident.”

Then I thought to myself, “I don’t think it would have mattered. There would have been something else.” You need to find something so you can’t focus on the story itself. If you do realize the nature of the story — forget about the misalignment, just the nature of the capabilities growth — then one, it’s just not a comfortable thing to think about. Two, it makes a lot of other priorities you might have, a lot of other topics you might want to focus on instead, much less relevant.

With regards to the plan, I’ve been reading these accounts of what has gone wrong in wars in the past. Ege, I know you’ve done a much deeper dive on these kinds of things. But why, for example, did World War I turn into a catastrophe? Why did America send troops into Vietnam? Why did we do Iraq?

What you find in many of these situations is that it was not as if the relevant political leaders got in a room and had a discussion about the pros and cons, the costs and benefits, how things could go wrong, for example, if we invade China, if you’re Japan, or if you give some security guarantee to Belgium, or if we send half a million troops into Vietnam: “What if things escalate in ways we don’t expect? Is that worth the benefits?”

Instead, what has happened in these cases, when people try to analyze why things went wrong, is that there actually never was a clear decision that was made in the first place. There never was an accounting of, “This is what could go wrong. This is what the benefits could be. Do we think it is worth it?”
Ege Erdil

And often the people who try to make that discussion happen get socially punished for it. For example, in Japan, there was a member of parliament, I forgot his name, but during the war with China, he stood up in parliament and was like, “Can someone explain to me what is the point of this? Why are we in this war?” Then they kicked him out of parliament. It’s just such an obvious, rational question. Why are we doing this? What is the point?
