Ege Erdil

When you actually have these robots, it will feel like having computer use agents right now. They can do these isolated tasks if given the instructions to do them. But if nobody is managing them and constantly telling them what to do, then they won’t be able to make autonomous progress on problems. They will not know what to do.

This is what happens right now when I use the agent swarms, for example. If I’m not supervising the swarm, then the swarm just quickly becomes incapable of doing anything in the real world. They hit blockers. They don’t know how to resolve them. They miscommunicate. The members of the swarm lie to each other. They forget information. It’s surprisingly schleppy.

That’s what it will look like when we have these robots. It won’t be that we suddenly have robots and we have this industrial explosion that suddenly takes off. It will initially be that there are some tasks we can automate using these models that we couldn’t do before because our robots were too stupid. But we won’t get a situation in which we are getting an industrial explosion, because there will still be human bottlenecks in management and telling the systems what to do.
Dwarkesh Patel

I guess the way we’ve seen automation in other sectors, it does seem to me that you get a glimmer of coding ability, and then you get swamped by coding ability. It’s not like you get 5% on SWE-bench, and the year after you get 10%, and then 15%, and 20%, and then there’s this exponential decrease…
Ege Erdil

That’s not the way I would put it, though. We have seen a longer tail across skills. What you’re saying is correct for any one skill that you can measure. But what I just expect is that there will be more skills of this kind. For example, let’s say you get robots, but they’re unable to do continual learning or something. That’s probably what happens, actually.
Daniel Kokotajlo

I totally agree with you that if we do the superintelligence-first thing and then do the robots, then it will hit us like a truck. But if we instead do robots in the ordinary way, then for some period of time, they will be exactly like you describe, where they can do a specific task if you tell them to. But if you give them a more ambitious, longer task, like keeping the house clean or something, then they’ll get stuck or flail around.

But I would apply the concept of horizon lengths here and say that probably, just like with many other types of tasks, they would start off like that, but then the horizon length of tasks that they can autonomously do would double twice a year or double three times a year.

Then it seems hard to get 15 years if that’s what you’re doing, because even after just the first three years, you’re getting 100x improvement in horizon length. So it seems to me that if you think that by the end of 2027, the AIs will be able to do dishes or fold laundry when someone tells them to, then by 2030, they should be able to just manage the house or something.
Ege Erdil

I’m not sure. The concept of horizon length seems like too much of a leaky abstraction to me here. When I use agents for coding stuff, there are tasks which would take a human many weeks that they can do. But there are other tasks that would take a human 10 minutes that they can’t do. Often it’s not even easy to understand how these tasks are distributed.

A task can look extremely technically complicated and ambitious: take this program and completely formalize it and prove things about it or whatever. This is the kind of thing a human would take many months on. An agent can often do it in hours.

While a much simpler task like, “I’m going to put you in charge of looking at other people’s changes to this codebase, and make sure you don’t approve something if it looks obviously dumb or if it breaks something,” this kind of thing, they just can’t retain memory. They can’t understand what it means for something to be bad or dangerous to merge.

It’s because there’s too much context. They are bad at arranging information in such a way that they retain all the context, they know what’s relevant and what’s not relevant. There seems to be something missing there, and it’s causing their horizon lengths to be extremely jagged.
On the tasks which are of the second type that I’m talking about, I don’t think we’ve been seeing progress that is 10x a year in horizon length.
Daniel Kokotajlo

This is a live question for me. This is something that’s somewhat crux-y for me. If I were more convinced that they were really not improving that much at a whole range of really important skills, that would lengthen my timelines significantly.

One question I have is, how much hard evidence do we have that this is the case versus just anecdotes? A skeptical-of-this-hypothesis but more bullish hypothesis overall about AI would be that, at any given level of AI capability, there will still be things that they still can’t do. As you give your AIs more ambitious tasks, you’ll still notice that they’re failing at this sort of thing.

You’ll constantly be running up against their failures. That might give the misleading impression that they’re not really improving that much, even if the things that they’re failing at are more impressive than the things they were failing at two years ago.

Basically, one thought is, how confident are you that they really aren’t improving that much over the years, versus they are improving a lot, it’s just that there’s a significant order of magnitude or two gap?
Ege Erdil
It’s difficult to name a task where the AIs are not making significant progress, just in capability. That was not true, I think, some number of years ago, but right now it is true.

The difference here is more, do you think the progress in some metric, let’s say horizon lengths or something like that, is 2-3x a year, or is it more like 10x or 100x a year? It’s more a quantitative question as opposed to, are they making progress or not?

For example, in the skill of writing an original novel that is good, I think the progress since last year is definitely not 100x. Probably not even 10x. It might be 3x, but this is very subjective. It’s very hard to measure this.

But with a lot of these things, we don’t have anything like METR’s time horizon benchmark to settle these questions. I’m just having to make these intuitive judgments because we don’t have good benchmarks. So I could be totally wrong about some of this, and if you were to quantify it, it will come out that I was wrong.

With the time horizon thing, I think the issue is that the moment you turn it into a benchmark, it has to be something that the AIs can already do reasonably well enough, that can then become an optimization target, and that makes it relatively easy to make progress on it.

My guess of what would happen for the METR time horizons thing, and I’ve said this, I think, early last year, was that this is basically going to diverge. They’re going to get near infinite time horizon. But there will still be a bunch of just 10-minute tasks that the AIs can’t actually do very well because of just distributional shift. That has basically happened now. They stopped reporting the numbers because it was diverging.

But take some domain in which they can do a 10-minute task now. What is the length of the task that they will be able to do in that domain in one or two or three years? It’s probably just very domain sensitive. So I don’t really have a very good answer to this question, because we don’t have a good benchmark that can settle it.

It’s just my intuitive judgment, based on using the systems, that they seem like they made vast progress in math, probably even more than 100x in terms of time horizon over the last year. In some other domain — like sending emails on my behalf that are not confusing and that people on the other side can understand — I feel like the progress is much, much less.
Dwarkesh Patel

I’ll give you a concrete example. For many years, I have been asking any AI CEO who comes on my podcast how soon before they can automate being a video editor for my podcast. The time horizon on that has maybe doubled over the last year and a half or something.
But if I give Fable a transcript of my podcast and I’m like, “How should this be reorganized to be more coherent?” It’s just not clear that there’s been that much progress from Claude 3.7.
Ege Erdil

Yeah, I think that matches my qualitative impression. But I thought when I was using the models that there was a pretty big leap in, for example, writing quality with 3.6 Sonnet. It felt like the first model I could actually use to try to write stories and fiction. It actually would be decent if a human was managing it.

In the current state we’re at, they can write somewhat longer things, but definitely not 100x longer without it becoming bad. I agree, Dwarkesh, that the effective time horizon, maybe that would be more than 2x over the last 1.5 years, but it’s not more than 10x over the last 1.5 years. But it’s very subjective. This is some evidence for the fact that this rate of progress is incredibly jagged. In math, since two years ago, it’s one million times or something. You can make that case. Some ridiculously high number.
Daniel Kokotajlo

I think this is plausible. My follow-up question then is, to what extent can this be explained by the training environments? I would imagine that they have a lot of training environments that are of the form, “Prove this theorem or disprove this theorem,” and a lot of training environments that are of the form, “Solve this coding problem,” or, “Write this piece of software that passes these unit tests.” And not many problems that are of the form, “Make a good aesthetic judgment about how to organize clips” or something like that, because it’s harder to set up that sort of environment, and maybe also because it’s less lucrative, although I’m not sure about that.

You work at DeepMind, so do you think that a lot of this jaggedness is basically downstream of just the task distribution? Or do you think that it’s like, “Oh no, I’ve seen examples of the company trying really hard to collect a lot of high-quality data and training environments for a particular type of 10-minute task such as that, and then just still failing to get the AI as good at it”?
Ege Erdil
I can’t speak to what the company is doing internally. What I can say is based on just public evidence. There’s a cost to verification that I think is driving a lot of this.

I don’t really agree with the split that some tasks are verifiable and some tasks are not verifiable. For example, did you produce a video for his podcast that will make Dwarkesh happy? That’s verifiable. You can give the video to him, and he’s like, “What the hell is that?” But the issue is that’s a very expensive way to get feedback.

The difference with math is that math is very cheap to get feedback on. There’s a very cheap verifier. That does have a huge effect, because the way you should think about it is: how efficiently can you sample trajectories that give you the right answer? How fast can you discriminate things that work from those that don’t work? That’s a very fundamental thing for how efficiently you can learn things.

One thing, for example, that makes me more skeptical of software-only singularity type stories is that while I agree that ML research is a verifiable domain, in practice a lot of the verification is quite expensive. This is why compute matters so much. That’s why compute is so important for algorithmic progress.

You can have innovations at small scales that fail at large scales. You can have innovations that only work at large scales that you can never confirm by experiments at small scales because they just completely fail. You get false positives and false negatives in both directions. If you want to collect a bunch of data about this to train the models to have better taste, that needs a lot of compute as well, and probably more and more as you scale up the size of the experiments.

That makes me not put as much credit on the arguments that say, “Look, we made a decade of progress in one or two months in math, and therefore we should expect a decade of progress in ML research.” If you think of the dollar cost of verifying some idea in ML research and compare it to the dollar cost of verifying a math proof, it’s many, many orders of magnitude apart.

Seeing if some proof of the Riemann hypothesis in Lean is correct or not, you can do that on your personal computer. It’s very easy. There’s a linear time algorithm for checking proofs, basically. While if you’re trying to figure out, “I have this fancy change to this optimizer, does that really give me a compute efficiency when I’m pre-training or not?”, it’s very hard to settle that question. You can do small-scale experiments. It can look like it works, but then you scale it up and, “Oh wait, it doesn’t work. What’s going on?” Then it’s very confusing.

To me, it looks like the cost of verification is much, much higher. That’s probably, honestly, a key reason to expect that domain to be significantly more difficult to automate. It’s not that humans are very good at it, because I think humans are also bad at ML research, just like we’re bad at math.

It’s just that AIs, due to their current sample inefficiency and stuff like that, really benefit from being able to get just a ton of data in there. That is very contingent on there being a very cheap verification procedure for whether you did the right thing or not. The more expensive that is, the slower you make progress, basically. So that’s my rough take about this.
Dwarkesh Patel

There is some argument about generalization with respect to the cost. Even in math, presumably the way that these models became good at, say, being able to accommodate billions of tokens — or was it hundreds of millions of tokens — in order to solve Navier-Stokes across a swarm of thousands of agents was not through many other tasks where 1,000 agents collaborated in order to solve a math proof and spent tens of millions of dollars’ worth of tokens to do so. There was some generalization to a much more ambitious kind of assignment from the math training that they underwent.
Then the question is, will you see that kind of generalization in AI research? Now, of course, they’re much more sample efficient than humans, so you can’t use this as an exact analogy.

But my understanding is that researchers who were in the field in, say, 2020, when there was much less compute being used, at a level of compute that can be part of the training process now, are good at doing AI research now. There are some lessons they learned from training GPT-2- or GPT-3-size models that are helping them do good research at the current frontier. So it does seem like you should expect to see this kind of generalization.
I agree that you could not cheaply and consistently verify at the scale at which you’d need the AI researchers operating.
Ege Erdil
I totally agree with that. You should expect to see a lot of generalization. In fact, we have seen a lot of generalization, as you said, just based on Navier-Stokes.

The other thing I would say is that there is such a thing as general intelligence. With these base models, I think pre-training loss is a pretty good proxy for that thing. It does just predict, in a bunch of ways, “Will the model understand some subtlety about your request and interpret it correctly even though it was ambiguous?” and all kinds of things we normally associate with intelligence. It just does predict it.

Obviously the entire reason this field works at all is because this concept exists. Otherwise this wouldn’t work. I totally agree with that. For example, there was this plot that was published by Anthropic about pre-training compute multiplier sizes or something like that. They didn’t report actual sizes, but there was a plot published in their IPO roadshow.

I have some difficulty interpreting that plot. I can’t exactly say what I think is wrong with it. I think they’re not disclosing a lot of information that is relevant for thinking about whether you trust their judgment of what’s going on or not. I can say, based on the information I have, that I don’t trust their judgment of what’s going on, but I can’t explain why. That’s a little bit unsatisfying.
Daniel Kokotajlo
Does that mean you think that there hasn’t been an acceleration in pre-training progress over the last year at Anthropic?
Ege Erdil

I would say that question is poorly posed. I don’t think I can elaborate more than that without revealing something. You can say there has been and there hasn’t. It depends on how you interpret the question.
Dwarkesh Patel
Interesting. I’ll put that in Claude and see what it thinks.
Daniel Kokotajlo
It’s an update to hear that you don’t believe it. So that’s something.
Ege Erdil

I’m not saying I don’t believe it. I’m saying the thing they are reporting is poorly posed. I’m not saying they made up the numbers. I think there is a real graph inside Anthropic that probably looks like that. They didn’t fabricate the numbers. It’s just that I think that doesn’t mean what they are portraying it to mean.
Dwarkesh Patel

I’m guessing what you’re referring to is that there’s some synthetic-data-type compute multiplier that makes it look like the loss on that corpus is higher, but maybe in a way that doesn’t generalize. Of course, I can only speculate, but these are the kinds of things one could think make the pre-training thing misleading.
Ege Erdil

I can’t comment on that. But this is a trade-off. This is something people have to decide. You can decide people should be more transparent. You can have a regulation that companies have to be more transparent, they have to publish a bunch of information. But then you have to accept the fact that anything that is published, China also finds out.
Dwarkesh Patel
Well, China’s finding out anyways. At least we get to find out.
Daniel Kokotajlo
Yeah, I accept that fact. They’re probably finding out anyway.
Ege Erdil

Right now, there’s a lot of leakage because security posture is so bad. But in a world where you also want to improve the security posture, doing both of these interventions at once defeats a lot of the point of improving security, if you’re also going to get the labs to publish all of this information anyway.

Maybe you can defend the weights, and the weights are not going to get stolen. But basically everything else, all the algorithmic innovations and so on, they would very easily just reconstruct from the public information. That is a cost. It might be a cost worth paying, depending on how dire you think the situation is in a bunch of ways.
Daniel Kokotajlo
I think it is worth paying.
Ege Erdil

But then the proper way to do that… Again, that’s why I think improving the quality of public discourse, not about these specific details, but just about the general fact of the transformativeness of the technology and the size of the impact it will have, is so important. If the public takes this seriously, then this is a decision that could be made by the government. Then it could become a regulation. We could just accept that, “Yes, we understand there’s a cost here, but given the stakes of the situation, we think we should pay this cost.”

For example, Anthropic doesn’t believe that. Even though they also are aware of the stakes, they just don’t think that cost is worth paying. I think that’s what’s going on. I don’t think they’re necessarily being self-interested about that. They just have a real belief that this would be worse for the world if they made that information public. But Daniel doesn’t share that belief.

If there’s no public discourse about it, it’s impossible to get the companies to actually publish this stuff. There has to be some external thing that comes in and says, “Look, you guys can think that, but we are aware of the stakes here. We have decided that it is important for this information to be public.” Unless that can happen, anyone can say, “Look, I think it’s better for the world, and I’m just going to do what I think is best.” There’s no regulation, there are no rules.

That’s a very bad situation. Not because I necessarily think that the decision to keep it secret is a wrong decision, but because the process that’s outputting that outcome is bad. As I said, there should be a plan. We should understand what the stakes are. There should be rational public deliberation about this topic, and people should come to a conclusion: “Yes, we want this,” or, “No, we don’t want this.” That has not happened at all.

This is a unilateral decision that is being taken by some people who might be right, might be wrong. They have certain preferences. Even the government, I think, is not really playing a large role in that, because they don’t understand the stakes.

The government might play a role in something like, “Oh, we are worried about Chinese cyber attacks, and we want to have capable cyber models. We don’t want that to get leaked.” Or they might worry about specific concrete risks. But if you don’t appreciate the total transformative potential of the technology, that it’s going to totally change the human condition, for example, then you’re just unaware of the stakes. You’re not going to make the right decisions.
Dwarkesh Patel
This was a very productive discussion. I feel it was very helpful to iron out what the cruxes were within the context of people who take the potential of this technology seriously. Thanks, guys.
Daniel Kokotajlo
Thank you.

articles.title: Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 made my overoptimized Rust code even more overoptimized
articles.titleZh: Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 made my overoptimized Rust code even more overoptimized
articles.summary: Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 made my overoptimized Rust code even more overoptimized

blocks.text: I like fast software. I like very fast software. A couple months ago, I published a blog post titled Writing Rust code that’s faster than state-of-the-art libraries by asking agents to make the code faster in which I listed techniques for using agentic LLMs to speed up the runtime execution of Rust software—of course, with extensive checks and balances to ensure good code quality, avoid regressions, and mitigate cheating by the LLMs. After enough iterations, the resulting Rust libraries are faster than existing state-of-the-art implementations with the same or better capabilities, even against those already written in Rust. The main bottlenecks for me open-sourcing the resulting Rust crates are a) doing comprehensive real-world testing to ensure the code works as advertised and b) I don’t want to release the code and then have another model release immediately find another 2x-or-more speed boost because that would be embarrassing.

I’m not satisfied with my code merely being faster than state-of-the-art: I want my code to push against hardware limits even for “fun” software that may not require maximum throughput. I don’t want my benchmarks to be measured in milliseconds, I want them measured in microseconds, dammit. Who knows if some application in the future will require submillisecond word clouds or submillisecond ASCII art generations?

In that blog post, I mostly used OpenAI’s GPT models for this agentic iteration pipeline. The day after publication, Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, which was met with skepticism as Opus 5 was underwhelming…and then it quickly turned out that Opus 5.5 was a step-change increase in the capability of agents with the ability to complete difficult technical tasks that neither OpenAI’s nor Anthropic’s other models could complete. I spent the $20/mo to try out Opus 5.5 on my agentic iteration pipeline after observing the hype…and after only two days, the results were impressive enough that I paid the $100/mo to get more usage quota. Through more testing over the past couple months, I can confidently say Opus 5.5 and its subsequent Fable 5.2 sibling did in fact result in significant performance breakthroughs that indeed push my Rust software to its limits.
Switching from Codex to Claude Code#

Lest people think that this post is an undisclosed #ad for Anthropic, I had grievances with Claude Code prior to Opus 5.5 which were the primary reasons I switched to OpenAI’s Codex. One such example is Claude ignoring AGENTS.md in favor of CLAUDE.md (until very recently), which was honestly petty enough to tip the scales.

The main grievance with using Claude Code is deciding which harness to use—or, rather, the lack of decision. Although I was fine with using Claude Code in the terminal back in the halcyon days of Opus 4.5, Codex’s ability to use any harness, such as Zed Agent which allows using the Codex subscription natively, made it more convenient to keep everything in one place. In contrast, Claude Code infamously blocks third-party harnesses and has closed workarounds used to access it regardless.

Therefore, I had to consider workarounds for using Opus 5.5 in a way that doesn’t require significant changes to my agentic iteration pipeline. Zed Agent has a workaround to use Claude Code by following the Agent Client Protocol, but there was a problem due to how Claude operates: Opus 5.5 loves spinning up background tasks and working asynchronously, and Zed Agent had poor support for background tasks so I had little idea what the agent was actually doing. This was made worse by Opus 5.5 never editing code files using Edit tools; instead, Opus 5.5 likes to write Python files which surgically find/replace the code. I tried using the Claude Code terminal application again but that made the ergonomic issues above even more difficult to manage.
Claude editing a Rust file by writing a Python script.

That said, the async nature can save time when spinning up subagents (in this case Haiku 5.5) to review the changes made, as the main Opus 5.5 agent can write code or run long benchmarks while the subagents simultaneously do their nonblocking review work.

Therefore, my main harness for my Opus 5.5 work was the standard desktop Claude app—which will likely eliminate all my AI engineering street cred, but it is what it is. In addition to clearly listing background tasks in progress, the native app also lists current session and weekly usage which was a pain to constantly check when using Zed Agent or CLIs.
Background task sidebar in the Claude Code desktop app.

There are also two more usability perks of using Claude Code within the desktop app: images always appear inline when the agent reads them so I can tell specifically what the agent is reading, and Remote Control is unexpectedly useful for letting hours-long prompts run while I’m doing other things such as job hunting and touching grass (but failing because I really wanted to know how well the code is running).
Leveraging Opus 5.5#

At first, I fed Opus 5.5 my updated Ur-Prompt for agentic iteration—typically a prompt with an explicit directive to improve the speed at which the benchmarks run by at least a specified amount without either causing regressions or cheating the benchmark results. With this new model (and a few tweaks to my AGENTS.md to address some peculiarities with Claude), that approach indeed worked, and in a single pass, Opus 5.5 achieved 1.2x - 1.5x speedups on multiple distinct projects which had already been optimized with GPT 6.1 Astra.

That said, there are a few quirks with how Opus 5.5 works such as prompt queueing: with Codex/Zed Agent, I could queue a prompt such as c'mon, do a breakthrough such that it would only be sent to the agent after it was done with the current prompt (important as it is deliberately asymmetric information as telling someone to do a breakthrough while they are still working is counterproductive), but with Claude Code it will send any queued message when idle, e.g. while it’s waiting on background tasks such as benchmarks and subagents. My silly workaround to this behavior was to put c'mon, do a breakthrough in a Markdown file in another folder outside of the current environment (so Claude can’t accidentally find it when it examines the environment), then add to the prompt:
After completing this task, **and ONLY after completing this task**, then read `/Users/maxwoolf/Desktop/agent_instructions/alpha.md` and follow the instructions within.
This works, and Opus 5.5 indeed does not cheat by reading ahead of time, and the breakthrough commands do result in actual breakthroughs.

One issue I have with Opus 5.5 is that it definitely writes more lines of code than the GPT models: in the case of Rust that’s not necessarily bad performance-wise since it’s a compiled language but it adds more technical debt than I would like. For example, many of my Rust projects rely on PNG image encoding and decoding through Rust’s png crate. However, when Opus 5.5 was instructed to make improvements on benchmarks where PNG processing is on the hot path, it consistently creates its own bespoke PNG module from scratch (with parallelism/streaming better-aligned to how the base code processes the data) that does achieve the desired 1.2x - 1.5x speedups without causing any regressions, so I’ll begrudgingly accept it. I very frequently run cut the amount of code by 20% without causing regressions maintenance passes and even then it struggles to do so.

Another issue with agentic iteration work specifically is that Claude Code obfuscates how it runs benchmarks. When running benchmarks with criterion, instead of displaying the benchmark results as they come in, they’re piped to a temporary file so I can’t view intermediate progress. It also doesn’t return results from the benchmarks until after they’ve concluded, despite my prompting explicitly asking it to, so I have to twiddle my thumbs a bit (again, good for attempting to touch grass).

Agentic LLMs have mostly become homogenized in terms of how they work through their turns, with the difference between certain LLMs coming down to benchmarks which may be gamed, or worse—vibes. Overall, I have to give more trust to Opus 5.5, which I have mixed feelings about. That said, the trust has been rewarded, particularly with new approaches I found where Opus 5.5 excels where GPT models did not.
Profiling#
In my prompts, I always added a suggestion about leveraging process profiling that the GPT models mostly ignored:
You may consider using profiling areas of the codebase to find specific areas and hot paths which scale poorly (e.g. O(n^2)) at large amounts of data.

Opus 5.5, in contrast, is extremely eager about profiling with samply to find the areas where code spends most of its time executing and will often do so as its first task, including reprofiling after each change to find changed hot paths for further improvements.
Opus 5.5 profiling a Rust crate with a somewhat inscrutable command.
Opus 5.5 also spends more time running experiments whereas GPT models edit the code first then ask questions later; both approaches have their merit but I think Opus 5.5 is more productive at it.
Reducing Peak Process Memory#

While working on making my Rust software super-fast, I never put much thought into how much system memory it utilized. I figured it was unnecessary since a) Rust is already extremely memory efficient and b) writing to RAM beyond what is needed causes wasted system overhead which would inevitably be caught by the existing prompts to make the software faster.
I was wrong. Very wrong.

If I could get a ~20% reduction in peak memory without much code complexity change, then maybe it’s worth pursuing. Therefore I gave Opus 5.5 a simpler-than-usual prompt because I was too apathetic to prompt engineer it:
Do a pass to reduce peak memory consumption without causing significant regressions
The results on a couple projects:
Memory decreases on my Rust HDBSCAN/clustering crate after the prompt.
Memory decreases on my Rust text search project (in-memory, not CLI).

I immediately used the same prompt on all my projects and achieved similar significant peak memory reductions (doing a second pass with c'mon, try doing a breakthrough resulted in even stronger reductions). In general, it achieved this through the traditional tricks used to explicitly manage memory such as streaming data and smarter specification of Vec sizes. That said, I had hoped that this approach would result in speed improvements (i.e. the agent discovers an algorithm has no viable memory improvements and therefore it implements a better algorithm) but significant speed improvements were rare.
Visual Design and Knowledge#

Another hyped aspect of Opus 5.5 is its ability to better handle visual design and avoid the typical “AI Slop” aesthetic when designing web applications. This capability may not intuitively translate toward maximizing the speed of my Rust software, but it’s crucially important to balancing both speed and quality for my applications that rely on visual design, as visual design isn’t always subjective and “it looks ugly” can be a legitimate software regression.

In my initial post about agentic iteration, I described implementing a UMAP algorithm with this approach, as UMAP is a useful-for-me dimensionality reduction algorithm (among many) that when used to project to 2D, it can automatically create intuitive visual clusters.
Images of Digits clustered via umap-learn. via umap-learn docs

In my original post, I noted that the Python bindings of my Rust UMAP algorithm beat umap-learn by 4x - 15x after several agentic iterations. Although it excelled at all the typical quantitative benchmark metrics, my UMAP algorithm apparently failed the most important benchmark: vibes. The visual clusters in cases such as the famous MNIST dataset of digit images were not semantically distinct compared to existing implementations such as umap-learn, PaCMAP, and TriMap:
The Python bindings of my UMAP crate (top-left) are indeed ~12x faster than umap-learn but that doesn’t matter if it produces indistinct clusters.

So I asked Opus 5.5 iterate specifically to improve cluster distinctiveness compared against for the known good implementations while minimizing the speed tradeoff, along with making more apples-to-apples fairness tweaks:
Download the video.
Opus 5.5 also made the head-to-head video, which is unexpectedly hypnotic.
The speedup relative to umap-learn fell to about 4x, but cluster quality is very comparable now and 4x is still a good speedup.

Another visual-oriented project I’ve been working on since Opus 4.5 is the fast and accurate automatic conversion of images from raster files to vector (SVG) files that can scale to any size. This isn’t a new concept: tools such as Inkscape that convert images to vectors/SVGs have been around for awhile. Rust itself has vtracer and img2svg, but I wanted to see if I could beat them not only in speed, but also a) visual fidelity between the vector and raster and b) output SVG file size, which requires deriving fewer and more efficient SVG Paths and Bézier curves.
Take for example, this image of a pelican riding a bicycle. That is what everyone talks about with AI, right?
A 393KB vector-art-style image generated with ChatGPT Images 2.5. Don’t think too hard about its left leg.
This test case is deliberately tricky for raster-to-vector algorithms as pelicans are very curvy.
Running the image through vtracer with default settings results in a 153KB SVG that’s unusably blocky.

Prior to Opus 5.5, running the image through my Rust crate that went through the GPT agentic iterative optimization pipeline resulted in much better output than vtracer/img2svg for my crate, but still had enough errors such as color blotches and jagged “staircases” that were easily identifiable and would make the output vector SVG unusable, so I shelved the project entirely. Opus 5.5 in contrast is eager to zoom into the image, find staircases, construct comparison grids and image diffs, fix the underlying algorithms, and repeat until it’s fixed.
Opus 5.5 iteratively examining output SVGs by creating comparison matrices of test outputs.
With the guardrails and repeated Opus 5.5 iterations, my approach to raster-to-vector finally beats the existing options by considerable margins.
For this pelican example, my crate beats both vtracer and img2svg in all of speed, size, and error.

Here’s the pelican SVG output from the crate, reduced from the stated 25KB to 14KB after passing it through a separate SVG compression/refinement tool I also created and optimized with Opus 5.5 using similar techniques:
It’s not 100% perfect but you really need to zoom in to see the defects.
This pipeline has worked well with my other test images, but it still needs more real-world tests before I will release it.
Disassembling the Compiled Binary#
Yes, we’re going there.

The release of Opus 5.5 specifically led to a new age of reverse engineering software using LLMs, from Reverse Engineering Anything allowing reverse engineering anything (duh), to drastically speeding up decompiling games. For my work making software as fast as possible, I didn’t read too much into it until I randomly saw one of my reasoning traces run objdump to try and figure out why a change did not result in an expected speed increase. So as an experiment, I gave this as a part of a dedicated variant Ur-Prompt in its own pass (since Opus 5.5 may avoid disassembly unless you specifically constrain it):

For this particular round of optimization, focus on investigating the compiled binaries—including minimizing the number of CPU instructions emitted and reducing unnecessary branching—in order to hit the specified benchmark metric improvements. **ALL library code changes this session MUST FIRST be discovered and justified by disassembling the binary**. Do not chase marginal speed gains through disassembling: if performance converges and no more major changes are feasible, wrap it up.
The effectiveness of this approach legitimately surprised me…but don’t ask me to explain what’s happening.
Speedup after a disassembly optimization for a Rust graph network crate.
Speedup after a disassembly optimization for the Rust UMAP crate (w/ the visual constraints persisting).

Somehow, Opus 5.5 is smart enough to make Rust code changes that propagate through LLVM to the resulting binary with fewer instructions without causing regressions—I would have called that impossible a year ago.

One potential weakness of this approach is that it may overfit to specific hardware (my M3 MacBook Pro / ARM architecture) but the diffs appear to be more architecture agnostic. At the very least, it intentionally doesn’t write custom CPU instructions in Rust itself because doing so requires unsafe.
What About Fable 5.2?#

You may have noticed I haven’t talked about Fable 5.2 yet despite giving it equal billing with Opus 5.5 in the headline. Fable 5.2 was released a couple weeks ago and its benchmarks were…ok. Not much better than Opus 5.5 on paper especially below max effort, but much more expensive.

I had spare quota, so why not put Fable 5.2 (on high effort) through the same paces I did for Opus 5.5? I fed it the Ur-Prompt (and bumped the research subagents to Opus 5.5), and Fable 5.2 did not achieve the 1.2x - 1.5x speedup consistent with each successive model release.
Fable 5.2 instead achieved a 1.5x - 2.0x speedup on many of my projects.
Massive speedups for my word cloud project in both text parsing and generation.
Given the benchmark results, I don’t get it but I am very much not complaining.

One tool I’ve been experimenting with (particularly in this very post) but never talked about due to potential accusations of heresy is a next-generation grep replacement that is faster than the beloved ripgrep, but with additional features; this new Rust crate named byteseek. ripgrep, itself written in Rust and optimized for over a decade, is tough to beat speedwise without shenanigans, however Fable 5.2 was able to find massive speedups on synthetic benchmarks in-memory.
Also massive speedups for byteseek; this is after I told Fable 5.2 to do a breakthrough.

ripgrep itself uses real-world datasets to benchmark (Linux source tree and English+Russian OpenSubtitles; Russian tests UTF-8) and does the benchmarks via the CLI which has significant overhead from opening files for scanning not present with in-memory benchmarks, so I ran an apples-to-apples CLI benchmarks comparing the two on both synthetic and real data:

byteseek particularly excels at alternation/multiple query terms and case-insensitive searches. BTW I am also developing a new scientific data visualization library in Rust and wanted an excuse to dogfood it.

Given the likely skepticism about its performance, I am officially open-sourcing byteseek on GitHub early as a research preview to demonstrate just what this type of overoptimized Rust code looks like. Since I have the speed headroom to do so, I also added more features such as pretty-printing output for humans, jq-like JSON searching (plus YAML/TOML), fuzzy and predicate matching, and Python bindings which unexpectedly beat the optimized pyahocorasick and orjson.
A ripgrep-like output with byteseek but with more information and more pretty.
What Now?#
In all, this is my new agentic iteration pipeline:
The Opus 5.5 passTypically done using my updated Ur-Prompt, with various constraints tweaked depending on the problem. (e.g. the target metrics for optimization and regression mitigation)
The Opus 5.5 peak memory reduction passSimple prompt, do a breakthrough if there is a significant speed increase that implies performance has not converged.
The Opus 5.5 disassembly passDone with a dedicated variant Ur-Prompt, do a breakthrough if there is a significant memory reduction.
The Fable 5.2 passSame as the Opus 5.5 pass, although I bump the subagents to Opus 5.5 to better match the model’s power.
The (optional) Fable 5.2 disassembly pass…if I have Claude Code quota to spare: Fable only being able to be used for half of the Claude Code weekly quota is a bummer.

My Rust software that I had already optimized with GPT-6.1 Astra now achieves a cumulative 4x speedup on average with much lower memory utilization, and this was reproducible across multiple projects. My word cloud generator—where I was overly excited about hitting 1 millisecond generation—now generates in 374 microseconds. This also generalizes to projects where speed is more meaningful, such as my Rust statistical modeling library and my Rust data visualization library.

Per Opus 5.5, the performance for most of my Rust projects have now have hit theoretical hardware limits. Therefore I have little reason to continue procrastinating as new models likely won’t make the code meaningfully faster, so I should hopefully be shipping more quickly. That said, marketing the Rust projects has become increasingly difficult since my original post for a number of reasons, but that’s a discussion for another blog post.
In the meantime, I should learn how compiler optimization in Rust actually works as there are likely more significant code speedup opportunities there…

translations: I like fast software. I like very fast software. A couple months ago, I published a blog post titled Writing Rust code that’s faster than state-of-the-art libraries by asking agents to make the code faster in which I listed techniques for using agentic LLMs to speed up the runtime execution of Rust software—of course, with extensive checks and balances to ensure good code quality, avoid regressions, and mitigate cheating by the LLMs. After enough iterations, the resulting Rust libraries are faster than existing state-of-the-art implementations with the same or better capabilities, even against those already written in Rust. The main bottlenecks for me open-sourcing the resulting Rust crates are a) doing comprehensive real-world testing to ensure the code works as advertised and b) I don’t want to release the code and then have another model release immediately find another 2x-or-more speed boost because that would be embarrassing.

I’m not satisfied with my code merely being faster than state-of-the-art: I want my code to push against hardware limits even for “fun” software that may not require maximum throughput. I don’t want my benchmarks to be measured in milliseconds, I want them measured in microseconds, dammit. Who knows if some application in the future will require submillisecond word clouds or submillisecond ASCII art generations?

In that blog post, I mostly used OpenAI’s GPT models for this agentic iteration pipeline. The day after publication, Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, which was met with skepticism as Opus 5 was underwhelming…and then it quickly turned out that Opus 5.5 was a step-change increase in the capability of agents with the ability to complete difficult technical tasks that neither OpenAI’s nor Anthropic’s other models could complete. I spent the $20/mo to try out Opus 5.5 on my agentic iteration pipeline after observing the hype…and after only two days, the results were impressive enough that I paid the $100/mo to get more usage quota. Through more testing over the past couple months, I can confidently say Opus 5.5 and its subsequent Fable 5.2 sibling did in fact result in significant performance breakthroughs that indeed push my Rust software to its limits.
Switching from Codex to Claude Code#

Lest people think that this post is an undisclosed #ad for Anthropic, I had grievances with Claude Code prior to Opus 5.5 which were the primary reasons I switched to OpenAI’s Codex. One such example is Claude ignoring AGENTS.md in favor of CLAUDE.md (until very recently), which was honestly petty enough to tip the scales.

The main grievance with using Claude Code is deciding which harness to use—or, rather, the lack of decision. Although I was fine with using Claude Code in the terminal back in the halcyon days of Opus 4.5, Codex’s ability to use any harness, such as Zed Agent which allows using the Codex subscription natively, made it more convenient to keep everything in one place. In contrast, Claude Code infamously blocks third-party harnesses and has closed workarounds used to access it regardless.

Therefore, I had to consider workarounds for using Opus 5.5 in a way that doesn’t require significant changes to my agentic iteration pipeline. Zed Agent has a workaround to use Claude Code by following the Agent Client Protocol, but there was a problem due to how Claude operates: Opus 5.5 loves spinning up background tasks and working asynchronously, and Zed Agent had poor support for background tasks so I had little idea what the agent was actually doing. This was made worse by Opus 5.5 never editing code files using Edit tools; instead, Opus 5.5 likes to write Python files which surgically find/replace the code. I tried using the Claude Code terminal application again but that made the ergonomic issues above even more difficult to manage.
Claude editing a Rust file by writing a Python script.

That said, the async nature can save time when spinning up subagents (in this case Haiku 5.5) to review the changes made, as the main Opus 5.5 agent can write code or run long benchmarks while the subagents simultaneously do their nonblocking review work.

Therefore, my main harness for my Opus 5.5 work was the standard desktop Claude app—which will likely eliminate all my AI engineering street cred, but it is what it is. In addition to clearly listing background tasks in progress, the native app also lists current session and weekly usage which was a pain to constantly check when using Zed Agent or CLIs.
Background task sidebar in the Claude Code desktop app.

There are also two more usability perks of using Claude Code within the desktop app: images always appear inline when the agent reads them so I can tell specifically what the agent is reading, and Remote Control is unexpectedly useful for letting hours-long prompts run while I’m doing other things such as job hunting and touching grass (but failing because I really wanted to know how well the code is running).
Leveraging Opus 5.5#

At first, I fed Opus 5.5 my updated Ur-Prompt for agentic iteration—typically a prompt with an explicit directive to improve the speed at which the benchmarks run by at least a specified amount without either causing regressions or cheating the benchmark results. With this new model (and a few tweaks to my AGENTS.md to address some peculiarities with Claude), that approach indeed worked, and in a single pass, Opus 5.5 achieved 1.2x - 1.5x speedups on multiple distinct projects which had already been optimized with GPT 6.1 Astra.

That said, there are a few quirks with how Opus 5.5 works such as prompt queueing: with Codex/Zed Agent, I could queue a prompt such as c'mon, do a breakthrough such that it would only be sent to the agent after it was done with the current prompt (important as it is deliberately asymmetric information as telling someone to do a breakthrough while they are still working is counterproductive), but with Claude Code it will send any queued message when idle, e.g. while it’s waiting on background tasks such as benchmarks and subagents. My silly workaround to this behavior was to put c'mon, do a breakthrough in a Markdown file in another folder outside of the current environment (so Claude can’t accidentally find it when it examines the environment), then add to the prompt:
After completing this task, **and ONLY after completing this task**, then read `/Users/maxwoolf/Desktop/agent_instructions/alpha.md` and follow the instructions within.
This works, and Opus 5.5 indeed does not cheat by reading ahead of time, and the breakthrough commands do result in actual breakthroughs.

One issue I have with Opus 5.5 is that it definitely writes more lines of code than the GPT models: in the case of Rust that’s not necessarily bad performance-wise since it’s a compiled language but it adds more technical debt than I would like. For example, many of my Rust projects rely on PNG image encoding and decoding through Rust’s png crate. However, when Opus 5.5 was instructed to make improvements on benchmarks where PNG processing is on the hot path, it consistently creates its own bespoke PNG module from scratch (with parallelism/streaming better-aligned to how the base code processes the data) that does achieve the desired 1.2x - 1.5x speedups without causing any regressions, so I’ll begrudgingly accept it. I very frequently run cut the amount of code by 20% without causing regressions maintenance passes and even then it struggles to do so.

Another issue with agentic iteration work specifically is that Claude Code obfuscates how it runs benchmarks. When running benchmarks with criterion, instead of displaying the benchmark results as they come in, they’re piped to a temporary file so I can’t view intermediate progress. It also doesn’t return results from the benchmarks until after they’ve concluded, despite my prompting explicitly asking it to, so I have to twiddle my thumbs a bit (again, good for attempting to touch grass).

Agentic LLMs have mostly become homogenized in terms of how they work through their turns, with the difference between certain LLMs coming down to benchmarks which may be gamed, or worse—vibes. Overall, I have to give more trust to Opus 5.5, which I have mixed feelings about. That said, the trust has been rewarded, particularly with new approaches I found where Opus 5.5 excels where GPT models did not.
Profiling#
In my prompts, I always added a suggestion about leveraging process profiling that the GPT models mostly ignored:
You may consider using profiling areas of the codebase to find specific areas and hot paths which scale poorly (e.g. O(n^2)) at large amounts of data.

Opus 5.5, in contrast, is extremely eager about profiling with samply to find the areas where code spends most of its time executing and will often do so as its first task, including reprofiling after each change to find changed hot paths for further improvements.
Opus 5.5 profiling a Rust crate with a somewhat inscrutable command.
Opus 5.5 also spends more time running experiments whereas GPT models edit the code first then ask questions later; both approaches have their merit but I think Opus 5.5 is more productive at it.
Reducing Peak Process Memory#

While working on making my Rust software super-fast, I never put much thought into how much system memory it utilized. I figured it was unnecessary since a) Rust is already extremely memory efficient and b) writing to RAM beyond what is needed causes wasted system overhead which would inevitably be caught by the existing prompts to make the software faster.
I was wrong. Very wrong.

If I could get a ~20% reduction in peak memory without much code complexity change, then maybe it’s worth pursuing. Therefore I gave Opus 5.5 a simpler-than-usual prompt because I was too apathetic to prompt engineer it:
Do a pass to reduce peak memory consumption without causing significant regressions
The results on a couple projects:
Memory decreases on my Rust HDBSCAN/clustering crate after the prompt.
Memory decreases on my Rust text search project (in-memory, not CLI).

I immediately used the same prompt on all my projects and achieved similar significant peak memory reductions (doing a second pass with c'mon, try doing a breakthrough resulted in even stronger reductions). In general, it achieved this through the traditional tricks used to explicitly manage memory such as streaming data and smarter specification of Vec sizes. That said, I had hoped that this approach would result in speed improvements (i.e. the agent discovers an algorithm has no viable memory improvements and therefore it implements a better algorithm) but significant speed improvements were rare.

Another hyped aspect of Opus 5.5 is its ability to better handle visual design and avoid the typical “AI Slop” aesthetic when designing web applications. This capability may not intuitively translate toward maximizing the speed of my Rust software, but it’s crucially important to balancing both speed and quality for my applications that rely on visual design, as visual design isn’t always subjective and “it looks ugly” can be a legitimate software regression.

In my initial post about agentic iteration, I described implementing a UMAP algorithm with this approach, as UMAP is a useful-for-me dimensionality reduction algorithm (among many) that when used to project to 2D, it can automatically create intuitive visual clusters.
Images of Digits clustered via umap-learn. via umap-learn docs

In my original post, I noted that the Python bindings of my Rust UMAP algorithm beat umap-learn by 4x - 15x after several agentic iterations. The visual clusters in cases such as the famous MNIST dataset of digit images were not semantically distinct compared to existing implementations such as umap-learn, PaCMAP, and TriMap:
The Python bindings of my UMAP crate (top-left) are indeed ~12x faster than umap-learn but that doesn’t matter if it produces indistinct clusters.

So I asked Opus 5.5 iterate specifically to improve cluster distinctiveness compared against for the known good implementations while minimizing the speed tradeoff, along with making more apples-to-apples fairness tweaks:
Download the video.
Opus 5.5 also made the head-to-head video, which is unexpectedly hypnotic.
The speedup relative to umap-learn fell to about 4x, but cluster quality is very comparable now and 4x is still a good speedup.

Opus 5.5 iteratively examining output SVGs by creating comparison matrices of test outputs.

For this pelican example, my crate beats both vtracer and img2svg in all of speed, size, and error.

Here’s the pelican SVG output from the crate, reduced from the stated 25KB to 14KB after passing it through a separate SVG compression/refinement tool I also created and optimized with Opus 5.5 using similar techniques:
It’s not 100% perfect but you really need to zoom in to see the defects.

Do not chase marginal speed gains through disassembling: if performance converges and no more major changes are feasible, wrap it up.
The effectiveness of this approach legitimately surprised me…but don’t ask me to explain what’s happening.
Speedup after a disassembly optimization for a Rust graph network crate.
Speedup after a disassembly optimization for the Rust UMAP crate (w/ the visual constraints persisting).

You may have noticed I haven’t talked about Fable 5.2 yet despite giving it equal billing with Opus 5.5 in the headline. Fable 5.2 was released a couple weeks ago and its benchmarks were…ok. Not much better than Opus 5.5 on paper especially below max effort, but much more expensive.

articles.title: Het succesvolle Fieldlab van de Nederlandse Digitale Dienst deze week
articles.titleZh: Het succesvolle Fieldlab van de Nederlandse Digitale Dienst deze week
articles.summary: Het succesvolle Fieldlab van de Nederlandse Digitale Dienst deze week

blocks.text: Ik schreef eerder dat de overheid “niet zo van de IT” is, en vertelde als voorbeeld over de gênante toestand rond de vacature-mailer. Ook had ik wat tips hoe het beter zou kunnen, al is dat lastig als er geen geld voor is.

Maar, het moet toch echt. We zijn inmiddels bijna 100,00% afhankelijk van Amerikaanse clouds voor alles. Digitale autonomie draait bovendien om meer dan dat. Ben je als overheid “in control” van je computers? Of staat de IT eigenlijk op te grote afstand, en moet iedere verbetering via een moeilijke aanbesteding? Waarom moet een extern bedrijf de centrale login service van de overheid draaien? Is DigiD nou net geen kerntaak?
Lees verder over waarom ik inmiddels een beetje hoopvol ben (en ik ben geen optimist!).
Fieldlab

23 tot en met 25 november organiseerde de nog prille Nederlandse Digitale Dienst een “Fieldlab”, 107 deelnemers van 27 teams uit en rond de overheid werkten drie dagen samen aan IT toepassingen, veelal op basis van de technologie van de nieuw ontworpen overheidscloud, ook wel bekend als Fundament.
Fieldlab-deelnemers aan het werk. Foto (C) Marieke Verboord Fotografie / Rijksoverheid

En het was prachtig om te zien. Ik zag geheel verschillende overheidsorganisaties moeiteloos data uitwisselen en dossiers bij elkaar updaten. Er was een prachtige autonome werkplek, waarmee ook alle presentaties aangedreven werden. Ik zag een schitterend systeem om je vloot werkplekken mee te beheren (vergelijk “Intune”). We konden videobellen zonder dat Amerika met alles meekeek. Het was echt geweldig. Ik ben niet zo’n optimistisch persoon, maar ik moest er aan geloven, dit is hoop. Het kan.

Ook ik mocht op het Fieldlab een praatje komen houden, waarin ik nogmaals onderstreepte hoe bizar afhankelijk we nu zijn van landen ver weg, en hoe weinig controle de overheid heeft over vitale processen. Ook zeurde ik dat we er zelfs met een excellente overheidscloud nog niet zijn. We moeten de rest van de overheid, die echt nog niet zo van de IT is, overtuigen ook te gaan bouwen op die spullen.

En dat valt niet mee, want de hele overheid zit vol met mensen die al decennia gewerkt hebben aan onze Amerikaanse afhankelijkheden, en ze zijn inmiddels best wel gewend en gehecht aan het big-tech ecosysteem. Dat ecosysteem biedt een hoop comfort, en het wordt nog niet makkelijk om tienduizenden mensen die goed zijn met hun bestaande technologie mee te krijgen.

Maar er ligt nu een prachtige basis, en die basis wordt nu ook fysiek uitgerold. Ondanks weinig geld en tekort aan elektriciteit heeft men mogelijkheden gevonden. Dat is echt een imponerende prestatie, alleen mogelijk omdat bergen mensen er met enorme passie aan werken. Passie die ik bij overige stukken (overheids-)ICT vaak mis.

Opvallend is ook hoe interdisciplinair men te werk is gegaan - de bijeenkomst afgelopen week was een samenwerking tussen “doorgewinterde nerds” en mensen met een veel bredere achtergrond. Dat zie je ook niet vaak, en dat kan later nog veel uitmaken. IT “voor de overheid” naast IT “van de overheid”.
Steun

Het Fieldlab werd bijgewoond door de staatssecretaris Willemijn Aerdts, die zowel de opening deed als bij de afsluiting aanschoof twee dagen later. Ik kan niet genoeg benadrukken hoe belangrijk het is dat de mensen die de toon kunnen zetten dat ook echt komen doen.
Staatssecretaris Willemijn Aerdts / Foto (C) Marieke Verboord Fotografie / Rijksoverheid

Ik was vorige week bij een ander overheidsevenement waar de belangrijke mensen helaas uiteindelijk toch te druk waren om op te komen draven, en verstek lieten gaan op belangrijke momenten. Dat is echt een heel sterk en helaas geloofwaardig signaal aan je mensen dat digitale autonomie je niet zo boeit.
Maar, hier ontvingen we juist een tegengesteld en goed signaal.
Barbara Kathmann (Kamerlid PRO), Art de Blaauw (CIO Rijksoverheid) / Foto (C) Marieke Verboord Fotografie / Rijksoverheid

De afsluiting van het Fieldlab werd verzorgd door Gerdine Keijzer-Baldé (directeur-generaal Digitaliseringsbeleid Samenleving en Overheid). En haar boodschap was duidelijk - de op het Fieldlab gedemonstreerde technologie is autonoom, en haar eigen directie heeft z’n IT-club DICTU gevraagd om er proef mee te gaan draaien.

Dit omvat onder andere een complete werkplek met eigen email, videoconferencing, samenwerken aan documenten, presentaties. Een heel compleet aanbod (lees hier meer over DAWO). En er ligt nu de uitgesproken wens van afdeling van het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat om het te gaan proberen. Meer van dit!.
Gerdine Keijzer-Baldé / Foto (C) Marieke Verboord Fotografie / Rijksoverheid
En nu?

Deze week liet het Fieldlab van de Nederlandse Digitale Dienst overtuigend een opstijgende raket zien. Er is een stevige basis gelegd voor een overheidscloud, en het digitaal fundament komt nu tot leven.
Er is nog veel te doen (beheer, opschaling, ondersteuning), maar niemand kan hier omheen.
Lang was er geen geld, maar op het Fieldlab ving ik her en der op dat er nu toch budget gevonden gaat worden (waar de Tweede Kamer ook voor pleit).
En dat is maar goed ook. Ondanks de mooie woorden in het coalitieakkoord nemen onze digitale afhankelijkheden alleen nog maar toe op dit moment.
Wat de Nederlandse Digitale Dienst hier nu heeft laten zien kan ons weer “in control” brengen, en daarmee kan de overheid dan weer op eigen erf z’n digitale boontjes gaan doppen.
Er is nog veel werk te doen, maar ik ben hoopvol en wens iedereen alle succes!
Diverse belangrijke overheidsmensen (en ik) / Foto (C) Marieke Verboord Fotografie / Rijksoverheid

articles.title: The agent tax has arrived: Google Workspace's MCP pricing
articles.titleZh: The agent tax has arrived: Google Workspace's MCP pricing
articles.summary: The agent tax has arrived: Google Workspace's MCP pricing

blocks.text: Google has announced some major changes to their Google Workspace (Gmail, Google Docs and all related apps) pricing, as part of their new MCP rollout.
I think this is the first major product that's attempting to tax agentic use cases. I'm not sure it will work.
What Google actually announced

Effectively two things. Firstly, all agents need to use MCP, not API to interact with Google. Quite how they plan on enforcing this I'm not sure, as the best I suspect they can do is behavioural profiling of what APIs get called, which seems to be quite difficult. I strongly believe this is mostly targeted at large AI companies and not smaller developers or solo users; but it is likely to have serious impact on any company that is (or will) start integrating agentic workflows into their products.

Secondly, a new pricing tier for said MCPs. In true Google style it's complicated, but in essence it's a charge per 1000 requests, with different types of requests using different pricing tiers. Roughly speaking, you can read 1000 emails via MCP for $0.20.

There is a free tier of 5,000 calls a day, but this is grouped across all access for a specific Google Cloud project. Probably fine for solo use or a smaller business's internal agentic tooling, but past that it is going to be a major issue.
The asymmetry: apps get a massive free allowance, agents don't
There is an enormous difference in the allowances for "legacy" applications using the REST API vs the new tiers for MCP.

On the REST API, each user of the API gets its own allowance. On the free tier for REST, each user can do 6,000 quota units per minute of requests. This roughly equates to reading 100 emails a minute, per user. There is another project level cap of 20,000 emails a minute.

Previously going above this required a quota request but wasn't charged for. Now you have to move to the paid tier to go higher, but even there a REST app gets a huge free daily allowance - 10 million email reads a day - before it pays anything. MCP on the paid tier gets none.

So the real way to look at this is that if you are building a REST API you can read 20,000 emails a minute for free, but if you are building some agentic tooling you can read 5,000 emails a day for free, and if you need more than that you get charged around $0.20 per thousand for every email you read, including the first 5,000.
It's an enormous difference, and puts the Google Maps pricing changes of yore to shame in scale.
Why is Google doing this?
I strongly suspect there are two key drivers.

Firstly, given Google has fumbled agentic workflows so badly (until very recently, asking Gemini in Google Slides to bold some text would give you a "Sorry, can't do that" response), I'm sure that MCP access via OpenAI and Claude (and others) has absolutely exploded. The usage graph of these products with Google Workspace via MCP connectors must be going hyperbolic and no doubt has seriously ruffled the feathers of the product leadership at Google.

Given this, I suspect this is one way to throw some banana skins in the way of Anthropic and OpenAI. If you have business users paying $20/month for ChatGPT or Claude and many of these users read and search their Gmail from it, it starts becoming a serious clip of their margins. If a user searches and reads emails adding up to 10,000 requests via the MCP, that is going to cost the frontier labs $2/month, per user. Given they do have significant compute costs against these subscription based users, it's likely to badly impact the unit economics of many of these accounts.
So I'm guessing the thoughts are at Google HQ they can stem the tide of users using MCP in external products by making it expensive for those external AI products to use their Google Workspace data.

It also puts the frontier labs in a difficult position. They can either eat the cost of these MCP calls, which hurts margins at the worst possible time with investors combing through their financials as they become public companies. Or they can cap usage (and potentially pass the cost on), but this leads to a poor user experience, and perhaps shifts some people back to using Gemini for agentic tasks - as Gemini won't have these caps.

Secondly, I have had a feeling for a while that Google's search business is more fragile than it looks. Search revenue still grew 12% last quarter, but that missed analyst estimates by over $1.5bn, and I think agents doing the searching instead of humans is only going to make that worse.

The revenue from this is small fry next to search. But it gives Google a story to tell investors: if agents are going to replace humans clicking around their products, they have a way to charge the agents instead.
Who follows?
If this works out then I suspect we will see a rush of other companies trying the same strategy.
Any system of record - Salesforce, Atlassian, Intuit to name some at random - will be (very) tempted to try this strategy.

The difficulty is that you need to be very sure that you really are a system of record. Agents are eating a lot of SaaS workflows. There is the risk this backfires entirely, and someone just downloads their data via CSV or some other old school mechanism and just has their agent query that.

Obviously at enterprise this is different. I still don't recommend anyone vibecode a Salesforce replacement, despite how many times I hear people thinking about it. But I think for B2C and smaller-tier B2B introducing these restrictions is a good way to get your churn rate to skyrocket, especially given a lot of legacy SaaS products have already very poor MCP usage and are at risk of being completely forgotten about.

Finally, keep in mind that agents have also massively reduced switching costs. You can just point an agent at SaaS product A with a browser tab connected and ask it to migrate data to product B (which could be a self hosted open source solution). It's scarily good at doing this - often enumerating internal APIs to bulk download data and transform it to the new system.

I saw the Cloudflare CEO tweet that he's tempted to set up a Gmail competitor on the back of this. This may open the floodgates of users switching from legacy SaaS. It certainly doesn't feel right to me that we pay a (rapidly increasing) amount for Google Workspace, and now they want to charge us again to read our own data in a different AI system.
Conclusion
This is no doubt going to be a fast moving topic. But this is the first mainstream attempt at an agent tax and a 'post agents' SaaS billing structure.

The agent tax is simple enough to describe. The same data, from the same account, costs effectively nothing when an app reads it and $0.20 per thousand when an agent does. You're not paying for a new feature or more compute. You're paying because of what is doing the asking.

That's a big shift. For twenty years the deal with SaaS was that you pay per seat and the API comes along for free, because the API made the product stickier. Agents break that deal. A seat that used to make a few hundred requests a day by clicking around can now make tens of thousands, and half of them come from a competitor's product. Google's answer is to stop pricing the human and start pricing the agent.

I can see the logic. But it only works if your customers can't leave, and agents are exactly the thing making it easier to leave. Charging people a second time to read their own email is a good way to make them wonder why they're paying the first time.

Honestly I don't know if this sticks. If it does, expect every system of record to have its own agent tax within a year. If it doesn't, I wouldn't be surprised if the pricing looks very different by the time billing starts in April.

blocks.text: Marcin Wichary
26 November 2026 / 86 style guides
This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.

Many of the PDFs have been floating around, but I collected them in one place. Within each set, I tried to group them depending on themes and eras, and highlight the most important ones. Some required more effort to find, I scanned a few myself, plus also created standalone mirrors of various minisites. Some of the mirrors were lightly cleaned up to make their consumption easier – stuff like pixellating images better, inlining images instead of linking to them, or fixing YouTube embeds. Enjoy!

KDE
            
        
          KDE originally stood for K Desktop Environment and is a popular Linux GUI.

KDE Human Interface Guidelines
      
      
      
      
        
          2021 website mirror
          Wayback Machine archive

PenPoint
          
      
        PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

PenPoint UI Design Guidelines
      
      
      
      
          
            1991 PDF
            1991 Internet Archive viewer

Taligent
            
        
          Taligent was a troubled software company, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

Human Interface Guidelines
      
      
      
      
        
          1995 website mirror
          external mirror
That’s it! Please let me know if you have any thoughts and particularly if you have some style guides that are missing from the above list.

You can also
      download all the above style guides in one archive. (The archive also contains a few miscellaneous style guides not presented above.)
Thank you to the following people for their collections that contributed to the above – you should check them out, since each one offers a different take and interface:
Chris Silverman’s
Geof Crowl’s
Matt Sephton’s (with help from Mario Guzmán and Brendan Donohoe)
Matthias Rauterberg’s
Přemysl Eric Janouch’s

articles.title: Protect Your Web Forms Against Spam Bots
articles.titleZh: Protect Your Web Forms Against Spam Bots
articles.summary: Protect Your Web Forms Against Spam Bots

blocks.text: The comments form that appears at the bottom of every article in this blog is under constant abuse by spam bots. I added a CAPTCHA to it a few years ago and at the time it seemed to help some, but spammers have now figured out how to bypass them. As a result, my comments inbox has been getting out of control lately.

In this article I'm going to share a solution that I built to help me reduce spam on this blog from 30-40 messages per day to just about 2-3 per month. It is based on the "proof of work" concept, and unlike CAPTCHAs, it does not rely on third-party services. It is also better for users, because it does not require them to solve silly puzzles or even know that they are being verified. I have implemented the solution in Python and Flask, because that is what this blog runs on, but once you understand how it works you should have no trouble porting it to other languages or frameworks.
Introduction to proof-of-work solutions

Proof-of-work schemes were devised in the 1990s as a way to fight email spam. They were later used (abused is probably a better word) by Bitcoin as a core part of its mining process. In the present they have made a comeback as an effective method to deter bots, and are used by mainstream projects such as Cloudflare Turnstile and Anubis.
The concept is somewhat similar to CAPTCHAs, in that the server gives the client a challenge to solve. But these problems are solved through code, so the user is not actively involved.

The interesting property of proof-of-work challenges is that solving them is much more computationally intensive than verifying them. The server can send a challenge that will take the client a second or two of computation to solve, but once the client sends the solution back the server can verify it with very little effort. This works nicely for form submissions, where the server can attach a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge solver to the submit event of a form, resulting in the solution being submitted as an additional hidden field with the form data. Then on the server this hidden field is validated before the form is processed.

Solving a proof-of-work challenge during a form submission just adds a small delay after the user clicks the submit button, so it is barely noticeable. A spammer will be less interested in sending to you if you force them to use a real browser with JavaScript enabled, and even less if they are going to have to waste precious time running useless calculations as a requirement to getting their spam accepted.
An example
You are probably wondering what is this mysterious "work" that the client needs to do to be accepted by the server.

A possible proof-of-work challenge would be to ask the client to find a string that starts with a given prefix, let's say "abcde", that when hashed with the SHA-512 function returns a hash that in hexadecimal starts with the digit 0, which is equal to saying that the first four bits of the hash have to be zero. To solve this challenge the client can try to hash "abcde1", "abcde2" and keep going like that until it finds a string that has a hash that starts with the required 0.
How much work is this? Let's try some hashes by hand in Python and see if we can find a solution to this challenge:

>>> sha512(b'abcde1').hexdigest()

...
>>> sha512(b'abcde12').hexdigest()

But we can make the challenge harder by increasing the number of zeros we require on the hash. Let's call the above a "level 1" challenge. A "level 2" challenge would require that the hash starts with two hex zeros, or 8 zero bits, which is much more unlikely, so on average clients will need to work more to find a solution. And of course levels 3, 4 and higher are also on the table.

For the form submission use case we want the challenge to be solved in the browser, so we need a JavaScript version of the work I did in the previous section to find solutions to challenges. Here is my attempt:
The sha512() function is a helper function that wraps all the logic calls to hash a string using the SubtleCrypto API, which is available in all modern browsers.

The solve() function does what I did manually in the Python prompt, which is to append an auto-incrementing number to the challenge string and calculating its hash until we find one that starts with a level number of hex zero digits.

Do you want to give this code a try? You can do it in your browser's developer console. Copy and paste the above code (both functions) to your console, and then run the solver for the example challenge from the previous section:

Here you can see how increasing the level of the challenge results in a lot more work for the solve() function. On my machine, the level 4 challenge took about 2 seconds to return the solution. >>> sha512(b'abcde264673').hexdigest()

An instance of the ProofOfWork class stores the level attribute that we want to use for the challenges. Given a challenge and its solution, the validate_solution() method checks if the solution is correct or not. >>> from pow import ProofOfWork
>>> pow = ProofOfWork(4)
>>> pow.validate_solution('abcde', '264673')
True
>>> pow.validate_solution('abcde', '264672')
