Flask integration

As I'm sure many of my readers know, on my Flask applications I use the Flask-WTF extension to handle form processing. So the next step is to wrap the code I shared above in a custom WTForms field that can be easily added to a Flask-WTF form. This is actually where the meat of this solution lives, so I'll go slowly to make sure everything is clear, especially for those who just want to learn the technique and are less interested in the Python and/or Flask bits.
Design

Before I show you the code to integrate proof-of-work challenges with a Flask application let me share how I designed this solution to work, as this is going to be helpful when you try to understand and adapt this solution to match your own needs.

The form will include a hidden field that is dedicated to the proof-of-work challenge. The JavaScript solver functions will be added to the page as well, along with a custom submit event for the form. The chosen level for the change will be rendered to the page so that it is known to the solver when it runs.

The user will open or navigate to the page with the form, and eventually they'll hit the form's submit button. Our custom submit handler will prevent the form from being submitted right away. Instead, the handler will send a quick request to the server to ask for a challenge to solve. The server will generate a new challenge using a random number generator and return it. The server needs to "remember" this challenge so that it can verify the solution later on, so it will store a copy of it in the user session.

Once the client receives the challenge, it will launch the JavaScript solver with it, and when the solution is found it will set it as the value of the hidden field. Then it will allow the normal form submission process to resume, so the form will be sent to the server, with the solution to the challenge stored in the hidden field. To complete the process the server will retrieve the challenge from the user session and verify that the value of the hidden form field is a valid solution to it.
Security considerations

Covering the security aspects of the solution is extremely important, now that we live in a world of constant vulnerabilities being exposed. It is generally a good idea to put as many restrictions as possible, to prevent loopholes that may allow a bot to bypass or hack our challenge verification.

The attack vector for this solution is a client that can somehow choose a known in advance challenge for which they have a pre-calculated solution. I could think of two variations on this potential attack: either the client finds a way to override the challenge chosen by the server with their own, or they reuse a legitimate server-generated challenge multiple times, which means they would need to calculate a solution only once.

To prevent the client from overriding the challenge that the server assigns, we are storing the chosen challenge in the user session. I intend to implement this solution for Flask, which by default stores user sessions in a client-side cookie. The session cookie is protected with a cryptographic signature, so the client will not be able to rewrite its contents. For systems that use server-side storage for user sessions, the chosen challenge is also secure.

The second type of attack is more tricky to defend against when user sessions are stored in a cookie, because the user can take a session cookie that includes a valid challenge, calculate a solution for it, and then ignore any new session cookies that the server sends with new challenges and instead keep submitting the same session cookie and the same solution. This is called a replay attack, and to prevent it we will give each challenge a short period of validity after which the server will not accept it anymore. We can store the challenge expiration time also in the session, since the client will not be able to change it.

Another option that can prevent replay attacks that can be used alone or as a complement to the expiration time is to store challenges that were successfully used in a database that can be searched to ensure that a repeat challenge is refused.
That is really all the potential threats I could come up with, but please do let me know if you find other ways in which my solution can be insecure!
Challenge generator
As discussed in the design I provided above, we need an endpoint that will return challenges to clients. This would be what we use instead of the "abcde" from the manual examples I shared above.
Here is a simple Flask endpoint that does this job nicely:

This uses the token_hex() function of the secrets package of the Python standard library to generate a random token of a reasonable length. To be able to recall this token we are storing it in the user session under the _ch key. And to make sure that this token is only used for a short period of time after it is generated, we add a _chexp key with the timestamp of the expiration time, which in this example I set at 15 seconds from the time of generation, which should give the client enough time to run the solver for 1-2 seconds and then submit the solution.
Custom field

Now let's write the custom proof-of-work field for Flask forms. A custom WTForms field is defined with three classes: a field, a widget and a validator. The field class is used to instantiate the field in the form definition. The widget and the validator are auxiliary classes that the field uses to render the HTML for the field and to check that the value submitted by the user is valid respectively.
Here is the validator class for the field:

The validator retrieves information that was stored in the session ahead of time in the challenge endpoint from the previous section. If first ensures that the timestamp stored under the _chexp key in the session is in the future, because if it is in the past it means that this challenge has expired and cannot be used anymore.

To perform the actual validation the class creates an instance of the ProofOfWork class I shared above, and sets the level, which is an attribute of the WTForms custom field. The challenge is retrieved from the session's _ch key, and the solution comes from the data attribute of the field, which is where WTForms stores the value that was submitted by the client. The validate_solution() method of the ProofOfWork class does the verification.

If the checks done by the validator are successful, then True is returned and that will allow the form to be accepted. In case of a failed check a ValidationError is raised to halt the form processing.
Next let's look at the widget part of this custom field:

The widget is in charge of rendering the field to the HTML page. There is a lot going on here, with a significant portion of the action being in JavaScript and HTML code that will be sent to the client.

The return value of the __call__ method is the code that will be inserted in the HTML page for this field. This is an instance of the Markup class, which marks the text given to it as safe, which is necessary to bypass the default escaping. To generate the code for this field I'm using an f-string, which is very useful as a simple template language, even though it has the drawback that all the {s and }s used in the JavaScript code have to be doubled so that they are not interpreted as an f-string replacement section.

The first line in the f-string renders the field as a hidden field. The attributes variable contains all the HTML attributes that belong to this field, including the id and name which are added even if they were not provided by the caller.

The rest of the code generated for this field is in a <script> block. First, the JavaScript solver code that we have in the ProofOfWork class is added. After that a handler for the DOMContentLoaded is defined. This is the modern way to attach logic to run after the page loads, equivalent to the $(document).ready(...) that you may have used back when jQuery ruled the world.

The DOMContentLoaded event handler retrieves the DOM field element, and then from it it gets the DOM form element, to which it attaches a submit event that will trigger when the form's submit button is clicked. The name of the field is generated in the f-string, since this name is known when the form is rendered on the Python side.

The submit event for the form starts by calling preventDefault() to halt the form submission. This is because the solution to the challenge needs to be calculated and included in this submission. Next the submit button for the form is disabled, to prevent the user from clicking it again and launching multiple submissions in parallel. After that comes the core of the proof-of-work flow, which starts by sending an asynchronous request to the challenge endpoint, which I called /_challenge above. This is done with the fetch() function, which is available in all browsers.

When the challenge is received, the JavaScript solver is called. Note how the level that is required for this challenge is inserted in the Python f-string, so it will appear hardcoded when you look at the source code for the page in the browser. The solution returned by the solver is added to the hidden field's value attribute.

Once the solution is added to the form field, the original form submission event handler is invoked to do the submission. This is going to cause the page to change, so there is no need to worry about re-enabling the submit button.
The last component of the custom field is the class that represents the field itself, which relies on the above two classes as helpers:

from wtforms import Field

class ProofOfWorkField(Field):
    widget = ProofOfWorkWidget()

    def __init__(self, level, label='', validators=None, **kwargs):
        self.level = level
        validators = validators or [ProofOfWorkValidator()]
        super().__init__(label, validators, **kwargs)

The job of this class is to hold all the components of the custom field. The widget class attribute tells WTForms what widget to use to render the field, and the validators argument in the constructor links to the validator. A common pattern in WTForms fields is that the caller can provide a custom validator, although I don't think this is super useful for this use case. The level that we want to use for this challenge must be provided as an argument when the field is defined, and it is stored as an attribute so that it is available in the widget and the validator as field.level, as you have seen above.
A complete example
If you made it to here, then congratulate yourself, we are almost done! All that is left is to write an example Flask application with a form that we can use to test everything.

Since this is going to be just a test, the form that we are going to use will have just a name field and a submit button. The proof-of-work field is independent of whatever else is in the form, so it can be added to any form no matter how complex it is.
Here is what the form in the example looks like:

from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms.fields import StringField, SubmitField

class TestForm(FlaskForm):
    name = StringField()
    challenge = ProofOfWorkField(level=4)
    submit = SubmitField()

Here you can see that I have decided to use a level 4 challenge, which in other words means that the client will need to find a hash that starts with 0000. If you prefer to use quicker or slower challenges you can change the level to suit your taste.
Now we need a Flask application with an endpoint that renders the form and accepts form submissions. Using the form class above I coded a short endpoint as follows:
Here the Flask application is created and then provisioned with a secret key, which is required because the user session uses it to generate the cryptographic signature that secures it.

The endpoint presents the form to the user when the browser requests the page, and then on submission it adds the name that the user provided to the template, so that it can show a confirmation that it was accepted. For a failed submission you would not see the name displayed, because in that case the form validation failure would cause the form to be re-rendered with an error message to give the user another chance to submit.
I assume you'll want to try this out. To make it easy for you to install this example below you have the complete application in a single source file, which you can call pow.py:
In addition to the Python source code you'll need the index.html template file. This should go inside a templates folder that is in the same location as pow.py. Here is the template:

Proof of Work Example

{% if name %}

Submission was accepted for name {{ name }}.

{% endif %} {% if form.errors %}

The form had the following errors:

    {% for field, errors in form.errors.items() %}
  • {{ field }}: {{ ', '.join(errors) }}
    • {% endfor %}
{% endif %}
{{ form.csrf_token }} name: {{ form.name }} {{ form.challenge }} {{ form.submit }}

For those who are familiar with Flask-WTF this template should look very familiar. At the top the page shows a message with the name that was received successfully in a form submission. This message is conditionally omitted when no form submission exists. Then the form is rendered as is standard for Flask-WTF and WTForms, including the list of validation errors, and each form field.

To test this example you have to install flask and flask-wtf as dependencies. My recommendation is that you create a virtual environment using your favorite tool and install these packages there. If you have no clue what I'm saying, then I recommend that you check out my Flask Mega-Tutorial first, then come back once you've learned the basics of working with a Flask project.

Once you try the example you are going to find that it isn't all that exciting, because you'll see a form that asks you to enter a name and submit, and once you submit it just shows you the name that you typed. The only difference with a plain form example is that you will see a slight delay when you hit the submit button. That's when the JavaScript solver is running.

If you want to see what happens when a bot attempts to submit to this form, you can try to submit with curl, which is actually somewhat similar to how bots do it. The following example submits the form with the name field and a made up value in the challenge field:
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/ -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -d "name=foo&challenge=dont-know"
The output from curl is going to be the HTML response. If you scan the HTML you'll find the section where the form validation errors are printed. You should see something like this:

The form had the following errors:

  • challenge: Verification failed
  • csrf_token: The CSRF token is missing.
In addition to the bad proof of work, this shows an error about the good old CSRF token, which is enforced by default in all Flask-WTF forms.

If you wanted to do this closer to the way the bots do it, you would need to send a GET request first, scan the HTML you receive for the CSRF token, then send the POST request including it. That should give you just one error about the bad or missing solution to the challenge. But if you wanted to provide a valid solution to the proof-of-work challenge, then you would need to read the JavaScript code and figure out what it does, and this is where I hope the bot operators will decide this would be too much work and isn't worth pursuing.

Let me know if this helps bring some sanity back to your forms. As I was saying above, it may not last forever, but for the last couple of months I have been enjoying near zero spam noise on my blog comments!

The attack vector for this solution is a client that can somehow choose a known in advance challenge for which they have a pre-calculated solution. I could think of two variations on this potential attack: either the client finds a way to override the challenge chosen by the server with their own, or they reuse a legitimate server-generated challenge multiple times, which means they would need to calculate a solution only once.

To prevent the client from overriding the challenge that the server assigns, we are storing the chosen challenge in the user session. I intend to implement this solution for Flask, which by default stores user sessions in a client-side cookie. The session cookie is protected with a cryptographic signature, so the client will not be able to rewrite its contents. For systems that use server-side storage for user sessions, the chosen challenge is also secure.

The second type of attack is more tricky to defend against when user sessions are stored in a cookie, because the user can take a session cookie that includes a valid challenge, calculate a solution for it, and then ignore any new session cookies that the server sends with new challenges and instead keep submitting the same session cookie and the same solution. This is called a replay attack, and to prevent it we will give each challenge a short period of validity after which the server will not accept it anymore. We can store the challenge expiration time also in the session, since the client will not be able to change it.

Another option that can prevent replay attacks that can be used alone or as a complement to the expiration time is to store challenges that were successfully used in a database that can be searched to ensure that a repeat challenge is refused.
That is really all the potential threats I could come up with, but please do let me know if you find other ways in which my solution can be insecure!
Challenge generator
As discussed in the design I provided above, we need an endpoint that will return challenges to clients. This would be what we use instead of the "abcde" from the manual examples I shared above.
Here is a simple Flask endpoint that does this job nicely:

This uses the token_hex() function of the secrets package of the Python standard library to generate a random token of a reasonable length. To be able to recall this token we are storing it in the user session under the _ch key. And to make sure that this token is only used for a short period of time after it is generated, we add a _chexp key with the timestamp of the expiration time, which in this example I set at 15 seconds from the time of generation, which should give the client enough time to run the solver for 1-2 seconds and then submit the solution.
Custom field

Now let's write the custom proof-of-work field for Flask forms. A custom WTForms field is defined with three classes: a field, a widget and a validator. The field class is used to instantiate the field in the form definition. The widget and the validator are auxiliary classes that the field uses to render the HTML for the field and to check that the value submitted by the user is valid respectively.
Here is the validator class for the field:

The validator retrieves information that was stored in the session ahead of time in the challenge endpoint from the previous section. If first ensures that the timestamp stored under the _chexp key in the session is in the future, because if it is in the past it means that this challenge has expired and cannot be used anymore.

To perform the actual validation the class creates an instance of the ProofOfWork class I shared above, and sets the level, which is an attribute of the WTForms custom field. The challenge is retrieved from the session's _ch key, and the solution comes from the data attribute of the field, which is where WTForms stores the value that was submitted by the client. The validate_solution() method of the ProofOfWork class does the verification.

If the checks done by the validator are successful, then True is returned and that will allow the form to be accepted. In case of a failed check a ValidationError is raised to halt the form processing.
Next let's look at the widget part of this custom field:

The widget is in charge of rendering the field to the HTML page. There is a lot going on here, with a significant portion of the action being in JavaScript and HTML code that will be sent to the client.

The return value of the __call__ method is the code that will be inserted in the HTML page for this field. This is an instance of the Markup class, which marks the text given to it as safe, which is necessary to bypass the default escaping. To generate the code for this field I'm using an f-string, which is very useful as a simple template language, even though it has the drawback that all the {s and }s used in the JavaScript code have to be doubled so that they are not interpreted as an f-string replacement section.

The first line in the f-string renders the field as a hidden field. The attributes variable contains all the HTML attributes that belong to this field, including the id and name which are added even if they were not provided by the caller.

The rest of the code generated for this field is in a <script> block. First, the JavaScript solver code that we have in the ProofOfWork class is added. After that a handler for the DOMContentLoaded is defined. This is the modern way to attach logic to run after the page loads, equivalent to the $(document).ready(...) that you may have used back when jQuery ruled the world.

The DOMContentLoaded event handler retrieves the DOM field element, and then from it it gets the DOM form element, to which it attaches a submit event that will trigger when the form's submit button is clicked. The name of the field is generated in the f-string, since this name is known when the form is rendered on the Python side.

The submit event for the form starts by calling preventDefault() to halt the form submission. This is because the solution to the challenge needs to be calculated and included in this submission. Next the submit button for the form is disabled, to prevent the user from clicking it again and launching multiple submissions in parallel. After that comes the core of the proof-of-work flow, which starts by sending an asynchronous request to the challenge endpoint, which I called /_challenge above. This is done with the fetch() function, which is available in all browsers.

When the challenge is received, the JavaScript solver is called. Note how the level that is required for this challenge is inserted in the Python f-string, so it will appear hardcoded when you look at the source code for the page in the browser. The solution returned by the solver is added to the hidden field's value attribute.

Once the solution is added to the form field, the original form submission event handler is invoked to do the submission. This is going to cause the page to change, so there is no need to worry about re-enabling the submit button.
The last component of the custom field is the class that represents the field itself, which relies on the above two classes as helpers:

from wtforms import Field

class ProofOfWorkField(Field):
    widget = ProofOfWorkWidget()

    def __init__(self, level, label='', validators=None, **kwargs):
        self.level = level
        validators = validators or [ProofOfWorkValidator()]
        super().__init__(label, validators, **kwargs)

The job of this class is to hold all the components of the custom field. The widget class attribute tells WTForms what widget to use to render the field, and the validators argument in the constructor links to the validator. A common pattern in WTForms fields is that the caller can provide a custom validator, although I don't think this is super useful for this use case. The level that we want to use for this challenge must be provided as an argument when the field is defined, and it is stored as an attribute so that it is available in the widget and the validator as field.level, as you have seen above.
A complete example
If you made it to here, then congratulate yourself, we are almost done! All that is left is to write an example Flask application with a form that we can use to test everything.

Since this is going to be just a test, the form that we are going to use will have just a name field and a submit button. The proof-of-work field is independent of whatever else is in the form, so it can be added to any form no matter how complex it is.
Here is what the form in the example looks like:

from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms.fields import StringField, SubmitField

class TestForm(FlaskForm):
    name = StringField()
    challenge = ProofOfWorkField(level=4)
    submit = SubmitField()

Here you can see that I have decided to use a level 4 challenge, which in other words means that the client will need to find a hash that starts with 0000. If you prefer to use quicker or slower challenges you can change the level to suit your taste.
Now we need a Flask application with an endpoint that renders the form and accepts form submissions. Using the form class above I coded a short endpoint as follows:
Here the Flask application is created and then provisioned with a secret key, which is required because the user session uses it to generate the cryptographic signature that secures it.

The endpoint presents the form to the user when the browser requests the page, and then on submission it adds the name that the user provided to the template, so that it can show a confirmation that it was accepted. For a failed submission you would not see the name displayed, because in that case the form validation failure would cause the form to be re-rendered with an error message to give the user another chance to submit.
I assume you'll want to try this out. To make it easy for you to install this example below you have the complete application in a single source file, which you can call pow.py:
In addition to the Python source code you'll need the index.html template file. This should go inside a templates folder that is in the same location as pow.py. Here is the template:

Proof of Work Example

{% if name %}

Submission was accepted for name {{ name }}.

{% endif %} {% if form.errors %}

The form had the following errors:

    {% for field, errors in form.errors.items() %}
  • {{ field }}: {{ ', '.join(errors) }}
    • {% endfor %}
{% endif %}
{{ form.csrf_token }} name: {{ form.name }} {{ form.challenge }} {{ form.submit }}

For those who are familiar with Flask-WTF this template should look very familiar. At the top the page shows a message with the name that was received successfully in a form submission. This message is conditionally omitted when no form submission exists. Then the form is rendered as is standard for Flask-WTF and WTForms, including the list of validation errors, and each form field.

To test this example you have to install flask and flask-wtf as dependencies. My recommendation is that you create a virtual environment using your favorite tool and install these packages there. If you have no clue what I'm saying, then I recommend that you check out my Flask Mega-Tutorial first, then come back once you've learned the basics of working with a Flask project.

Once you try the example you are going to find that it isn't all that exciting, because you'll see a form that asks you to enter a name and submit, and once you submit it just shows you the name that you typed. The only difference with a plain form example is that you will see a slight delay when you hit the submit button. That's when the JavaScript solver is running.

If you want to see what happens when a bot attempts to submit to this form, you can try to submit with curl, which is actually somewhat similar to how bots do it. The following example submits the form with the name field and a made up value in the challenge field:
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/ -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -d "name=foo&challenge=dont-know"
The output from curl is going to be the HTML response. If you scan the HTML you'll find the section where the form validation errors are printed. You should see something like this:

The form had the following errors:

  • challenge: Verification failed
  • csrf_token: The CSRF token is missing.
In addition to the bad proof of work, this shows an error about the good old CSRF token, which is enforced by default in all Flask-WTF forms.

If you wanted to do this closer to the way the bots do it, you would need to send a GET request first, scan the HTML you receive for the CSRF token, then send the POST request including it. That should give you just one error about the bad or missing solution to the challenge. But if you wanted to provide a valid solution to the proof-of-work challenge, then you would need to read the JavaScript code and figure out what it does, and this is where I hope the bot operators will decide this would be too much work and isn't worth pursuing.
